meta.blurb: One ordinary day, twelve-year-old Kofi rides his bike, watches a kettle boil and looks at the stars, and his Aunt Zainab, a physics teacher, shows him the six big ideas behind all of it.
meta.bible: Kofi: a curious boy of twelve who asks plain questions. Aunt Zainab: his aunt, a physics teacher, patient, funny and warm. They spend one day together, from the morning bike ride to the night sky, in a small town with a park, a hill and a river. The six ideas, in order, are Motion and forces, Energy, Heat and disorder, Waves, Electricity and magnetism, and Atoms and the very small. New in the full-length book: Ama, Kofi's friend and neighbour, who has a skateboard and a toy rocket. Mr Boateng, who keeps the corner shop. Biscuit, Ama's dog. Mrs Owusu, the old neighbour with a very old radio. The day runs from breakfast to the stars, in twenty chapters. Voice: friendly, concrete and simple, with everyday examples; every fact is true and rounded with "about". beats.scene: Kofi and Aunt Zainab at a breakfast table with a bicycle outside the window
beats.summary: Kofi asks what physics is, and Zainab says six big ideas explain his day.

beats.scene: Zainab writes six short headings on the back of an envelope
beats.summary: Zainab lists the six ideas: motion and forces, energy, heat, waves, electricity and magnetism, atoms.

beats.scene: Kofi frowns at the envelope while his cereal gets soggy
beats.summary: Kofi worries that he is too young, and Zainab says physics begins with a child's questions.

beats.scene: Zainab drops a spoon on the table and Kofi watches it fall
beats.summary: Zainab says physics is asking why things happen and then testing the answer.

beats.scene: Kofi measures the breakfast table with a long yellow tape measure
beats.summary: Physics needs measuring: the metre, the second and the kilogram are the basic units.

beats.scene: Kofi times a rolling orange down the table with a stopwatch
beats.summary: Numbers let us predict: with distance and time we can find speed.

beats.scene: A notebook with a crossed-out guess and a new one written beside it
beats.summary: In physics an idea must agree with experiments, however famous the person who suggested it.

beats.scene: A bowl of cereal, a toaster and a steaming mug on the table
beats.summary: Even breakfast contains all six ideas, from moving spoons to hidden atoms.

beats.scene: A rucksack packed with a notebook, a magnet, a balloon and a stopwatch
beats.summary: Zainab packs the tools for the day: a notebook, a stopwatch, a magnet and a balloon.

beats.scene: Kofi wheels his bicycle out of the front door into the morning sun
beats.summary: They step outside, and the first idea waits: why things move the way they do.

beats.scene: A parked bicycle stands still on a flat road with a boy beside it
beats.summary: Things stay still or keep moving the same way unless a force changes that.

beats.scene: Kofi gives the bicycle a push and it rolls away down the flat road
beats.summary: A moving object keeps going until a force such as friction slows it.

beats.scene: Zainab pulls a card from under a coin balanced on a glass
beats.summary: Objects resist changes in their motion, a property called inertia.

beats.scene: A car stops suddenly and a bag on the back seat slides forward
beats.summary: Inertia is why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes, and why seat belts matter.

beats.scene: Kofi pedals down the road while Zainab walks beside him with a stopwatch
beats.summary: Speed is the distance travelled divided by the time taken.

beats.scene: Kofi on a bike and Ama on a skateboard pass each other
beats.summary: Velocity is speed with a direction, so the same speed can give different velocities.

beats.scene: Kofi starts from a standing position and pedals faster and faster
beats.summary: Acceleration is any change in velocity, such as speeding up.

beats.scene: A cyclist leans into a curve on a round road at steady speed
beats.summary: Going round a bend at steady speed is still acceleration, because the direction changes.

beats.scene: A chart with a line rising steadily and Kofi's finger on the numbers
beats.summary: Acceleration is measured as the change in speed in each second.

beats.scene: A hand pushing a bicycle seat and an arrow showing the direction of force
beats.summary: A force is a push or a pull, and it changes motion; it is measured in newtons.

beats.scene: Kofi pushes a loaded cart and an empty cart outside Mr Boateng's shop
beats.summary: A bigger force gives more acceleration, and a bigger mass gives less.

beats.scene: Kofi pushes the same empty cart gently and then with all his strength
beats.summary: The harder you push, the faster an object accelerates.

beats.scene: Zainab writes force equals mass times acceleration on a paper bag
beats.summary: Newton's second law links the three: force equals mass times acceleration.

beats.scene: A ten kilogram box on the pavement with an arrow of twenty newtons
beats.summary: A force of twenty newtons on ten kilograms gives an acceleration of two metres per second, every second.

beats.scene: A tennis ball and a heavy ball in front of a kicking foot
beats.summary: The same kick sends a light ball far and a heavy ball only a little way.

beats.scene: Two teams pull equally on a rope at the school field
beats.summary: When forces on an object are balanced, there is no change in its motion.

beats.scene: One team slips and the rope suddenly speeds toward the other side
beats.summary: The net force decides the motion: an unbalanced force changes velocity.

beats.scene: Kofi pushes a wall and slides backward on his skateboard
beats.summary: Every force has an equal force pushing back, which is Newton's third law.

beats.scene: A balloon rushes along a string stretched across the garden
beats.summary: A balloon flies forward because it pushes air backward.

beats.scene: A rocket rises on a column of fire above the launch pad
beats.summary: A rocket works by throwing hot gas backward, even in the emptiness of space.

beats.scene: Kofi squeezes the brakes, and the bike slows with a faint squeal
beats.summary: Friction slows moving things and turns movement into heat.

beats.scene: Kofi's rubber shoes grip the pavement while a wet board slides away
beats.summary: Friction is also useful: it lets shoes, tyres and hands grip.

beats.scene: Kofi rubs his hands together and holds them to his cheeks
beats.summary: Rubbing makes heat because friction turns movement into warmth.

beats.scene: An apple falls from a tree toward a boy in a garden
beats.summary: Gravity is the pull between objects, and the huge Earth pulls everything toward its centre.

beats.scene: Kofi drops a heavy ball and a light ball from a low wall
beats.summary: Gravity makes all objects fall at the same rate when air does not get in the way.

beats.scene: A feather and a hammer lie together on the grey dust of the Moon
beats.summary: A feather falls slowly only because of air; on the Moon, it falls as fast as a hammer.

beats.scene: A stone falling past a ruler with marks showing the speed growing
beats.summary: Near the Earth a falling object gains about ten metres per second of speed every second.

beats.scene: A parachutist floats down under a wide round parachute
beats.summary: Air resistance grows with speed until it balances gravity, so a falling thing stops speeding up.

beats.scene: The Moon rides in the blue sky with a curved arrow around the Earth
beats.summary: The Moon stays in orbit because it is always falling around the Earth.

beats.scene: Kofi stands on a weighing scale with the Moon behind him
beats.summary: Mass is the amount of matter, while weight is the pull of gravity on it.

beats.scene: A bright noon with Kofi and Zainab sitting on a park bench with lunch
beats.summary: Energy is the ability to cause change, and it comes in many forms.

beats.scene: A lamp, a fire, a battery, a drum and a stretched spring
beats.summary: Energy takes many forms, such as movement, heat, light, sound and stored energy.

beats.scene: A cyclist races down a road and another goes slowly beside it
beats.summary: Moving things have kinetic energy, which depends on mass and speed.

beats.scene: A car doubling its speed on a road beside a school sign
beats.summary: Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times greater.

beats.scene: A heavy lorry and a bicycle travel side by side at the same speed
beats.summary: At the same speed a heavier object has more kinetic energy, so it is harder to stop.

beats.scene: A roller coaster car waits at the very top of a high track
beats.summary: Raised things have stored potential energy that can turn into movement.

beats.scene: Kofi pushes his bicycle up the steep hill with a bag on his back
beats.summary: Lifting something higher stores more energy, and heavier things need more.

beats.scene: A catapult made of a rubber band stretched back between two fingers
beats.summary: A stretched spring or rubber band stores elastic energy that is released when it springs back.

beats.scene: A small apple being lifted one metre above a hand
beats.summary: A joule is the energy needed to lift a small apple about one metre.

beats.scene: The top of the hill with the town and the winding road far below
beats.summary: At the top of the hill the bicycle holds its stored energy, ready to be used on the way down.

beats.scene: Kofi freewheels down the hill with his feet off the pedals
beats.summary: Going downhill, stored energy turns into movement and the bicycle speeds up.

beats.scene: A stone on a string swings like a pendulum from a low branch
beats.summary: A swinging pendulum keeps trading stored energy for movement, and back again.

beats.scene: A scale with potential and kinetic energy balanced equally in the pans
beats.summary: Energy changes form, but the total stays the same.

beats.scene: A pendulum at rest and a hand touching its warm pivot
beats.summary: A real pendulum slows down because some energy becomes heat, but the energy is not lost.

beats.scene: Two roller coaster hills, the second one lower than the first
beats.summary: Roller coaster hills get lower along the ride because some energy always becomes heat.

beats.scene: A rubber ball bouncing lower each time on a paved path
beats.summary: A bouncing ball rises less each time because some energy becomes heat and sound.

beats.scene: A strange machine of wheels and weights with a crossed-out sign above it
beats.summary: A machine that runs for ever without a fuel cannot work, because it would create energy.

beats.scene: A bicycle lamp glowing as the back wheel turns and touches a small roller
beats.summary: Energy passes along a chain: from food to legs, to movement, and to light in a bicycle lamp.

beats.scene: A row of marbles, the first rolling in and the last shooting out
beats.summary: In a collision, energy and movement pass from one object to another.

beats.scene: Kofi writing in his notebook beneath the swinging stone
beats.summary: Energy is like money in the bank: it can be moved between accounts, but never made or lost.

beats.scene: Kofi eats a sandwich while a diagram shows energy flowing to his legs
beats.summary: Food gives the body chemical energy to move and to stay warm.

beats.scene: A sandwich with a glowing number beside it showing a million joules
beats.summary: A single sandwich holds well over a million joules of chemical energy.

beats.scene: Kofi holding up a glowing light bulb as a joke beside his chest
beats.summary: A resting person gives off heat at about the rate of a bright light bulb, roughly one hundred watts.

beats.scene: A light bulb and a kettle with a dial showing power
beats.summary: Power is the rate at which energy is used, and it is measured in watts.

beats.scene: An electricity meter with a bill and a clock beside a kettle
beats.summary: The cost of using energy depends on both the power and the time.

beats.scene: A car at a petrol pump beside black lumps of coal and a barrel
beats.summary: Coal, oil and gas are fuels that hold ancient sunlight stored by long-dead plants and animals.

beats.scene: A green leaf in bright sun with arrows of light entering it
beats.summary: Plants capture sunlight and store its energy in food, which is how most life is fuelled.

beats.scene: A wind turbine, a solar panel and a sunny sky above a field
beats.summary: Wind, rain-fed rivers and sunshine are energy sources that all come from the Sun.

beats.scene: Waves washing a shore beneath the Moon, and steam rising from a rock
beats.summary: Some energy comes from elsewhere: tides come from the Moon's pull and heat from deep in the Earth.

beats.scene: A bright modern bulb beside an old bulb that glows hot
beats.summary: Using energy wisely means wasting less, such as choosing efficient bulbs and switching off.

beats.scene: Steam rises from a boiling kettle in Zainab's warm afternoon kitchen
beats.summary: Heat is the movement of the tiny molecules inside things.

beats.scene: Ink spreads fast in a glass of hot water, slowly in cold
beats.summary: Molecules move faster in hot things, so ink spreads quickly in hot water.

beats.scene: A thermometer in a mug of tea and a bath of cool water
beats.summary: Temperature measures how fast molecules move, while heat is the energy that flows.

beats.scene: A thermometer with marks for freezing water and boiling water
beats.summary: On the Celsius scale water freezes at zero and boils at one hundred degrees.

beats.scene: A kettle with a measuring jug and a clock showing three minutes
beats.summary: Heating a litre of water to boiling takes about three hundred and fifty thousand joules, or three minutes in a strong kettle.

beats.scene: A hot sandy beach next to a cool blue sea under the same sun
beats.summary: Water needs a lot of energy to warm up, so the sea stays cooler than the sand.

beats.scene: Three jars labelled ice, water and steam with the same blue dots inside
beats.summary: Ice, water and steam are the same molecules in different states.

beats.scene: Ice cubes floating in a glass of lemonade on a warm table
beats.summary: Melting ice takes in heat without getting warmer, which is why ice cools a drink so well.

beats.scene: A pan of water boiling high on a snowy mountain
beats.summary: Water boils at a lower temperature on a high mountain, where the air is thinner.

beats.scene: A hot runner with drops of sweat and a boy blowing across his tea
beats.summary: Evaporation cools: the fastest molecules leave, so sweating and blowing on tea cool us down.

beats.scene: A metal spoon in hot tea with the handle growing warm
beats.summary: Heat always flows from hot things to colder things.

beats.scene: Kofi touches a metal table leg and a wooden chair leg
beats.summary: Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature because it carries heat away faster.

beats.scene: A metal saucepan on a stove with arrows along the metal to the handle
beats.summary: In conduction, vibrating molecules pass energy to their neighbours through a solid.

beats.scene: A woollen jumper, a double window and a thermos flask on a table
beats.summary: Insulators such as wool, trapped air and a vacuum flask slow the flow of heat.

beats.scene: A hot air balloon rising over fields above a small flame
beats.summary: In convection, warm fluids rise and cool ones sink, carrying heat with them.

beats.scene: A room with a radiator and arrows of warm air curling upward
beats.summary: A radiator heats a room by convection currents that circulate warm air.

beats.scene: The Sun shines across empty space and a hand warms by a fire
beats.summary: Radiation carries heat as invisible rays, even across empty space.

beats.scene: A white shirt and a black shirt hanging side by side in bright sun
beats.summary: Dark things absorb radiation and get hot, while light, shiny things reflect it.

beats.scene: A mug of tea cooling beside a thermometer on the wall
beats.summary: Heat flows until things reach the same temperature, a state called equilibrium.

beats.scene: A frozen night above ice, with a thermometer showing a very low number
beats.summary: Absolute zero, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, is the coldest temperature possible.

beats.scene: Milk spreads into coffee in a cup, with swirls that never go back
beats.summary: Disorder tends to grow, and mixed things do not unmix by themselves.

beats.scene: A tidy bedroom beside the same bedroom with clothes and toys everywhere
beats.summary: There are far more messy arrangements than tidy ones, so things drift toward disorder.

beats.scene: A shuffled pack of cards spread on the table, with one neat sorted row
beats.summary: Entropy measures how many ways the parts of something can be arranged, and it tends to increase.

beats.scene: A hot cup cooling while arrows of warmth spread outward into the air
beats.summary: Heat spreads out from hot places to cold ones, making energy more evenly spread and less useful.

beats.scene: A car engine with heat rising from the bonnet and a temperature gauge
beats.summary: An engine cannot turn all heat into useful work.

beats.scene: A pie chart of petrol energy with a small slice for movement
beats.summary: A petrol car turns only about a quarter to a third of its fuel energy into movement.

beats.scene: An open fridge with a warm grille and arrows of heat leaving
beats.summary: A fridge pumps heat out of its cold inside, using energy, and warms the kitchen in the process.

beats.scene: A cup falls from a table and breaks on the floor
beats.summary: Because entropy grows, we can tell which way time runs: broken cups do not mend themselves.

beats.scene: A green plant and a growing child, with sunlight arriving and warm air leaving
beats.summary: Living things build order using energy from the Sun and give out heat, so entropy still grows overall.

beats.scene: Kofi and Zainab walk toward the river with long shadows beside them
beats.summary: The third idea in a sentence: heat flows from hot to cold, and the world drifts toward disorder; then they set off for the river.

beats.scene: Kofi and Zainab sit by a pond as ripples spread out from a stone
beats.summary: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy without carrying matter along.

beats.scene: Two children hold a long rope and send a bump along it
beats.summary: A wave on a rope shows the shape moving along while each piece of rope only moves up and down.

beats.scene: A spring toy on the grass with a squeezed patch moving along it
beats.summary: In a longitudinal wave the pushes and pulls run in the same direction as the wave.

beats.scene: A drawing of a wavy line with the crest, trough and wavelength marked
beats.summary: A wave has a crest, a trough, a wavelength and an amplitude.

beats.scene: A stopwatch beside the pond while ripples pass a marker twice each second
beats.summary: Frequency is the number of waves each second, measured in hertz; speed equals frequency times wavelength.

beats.scene: A huge wave crossing a deep ocean beneath a small ship
beats.summary: Waves can travel very fast, and deep-ocean tsunami waves move at the speed of a jet plane.

beats.scene: Two stones dropped close together make two sets of ripples that overlap
beats.summary: Two waves that meet add up and pass through each other, which is called interference.

beats.scene: Ripples bounce back from the stone edge of the pond
beats.summary: Waves bounce off a barrier, which is reflection.

beats.scene: Ripples pass through a narrow gap in a wall and spread into half circles
beats.summary: Waves spread out when they pass through a small gap, which is diffraction.

beats.scene: A seismograph needle tracing wiggles beside a drawing of the Earth cut open
beats.summary: Earthquake waves travel through the Earth and tell us what is inside it.

beats.scene: A flash of lightning over distant hills and a boy counting on his fingers
beats.summary: Sound is a wave of vibrating air that travels much more slowly than light.

beats.scene: Kofi hums with his fingers on his throat, feeling the buzz
beats.summary: Sound is made by vibrations, which pass through the air as a wave.

beats.scene: A bell ringing inside a glass jar with the air being pumped out
beats.summary: Sound needs something to travel through, so there is no sound in empty space.

beats.scene: A boy listens with his ear against a metal railing
beats.summary: Sound travels faster in water and in solids than in air.

beats.scene: A guitar string vibrating, with a quiet low note and a loud high note
beats.summary: Pitch depends on frequency, and loudness depends on the size of the wave.

beats.scene: Biscuit the dog lifts his ears beside a bat flying in the dusk
beats.summary: Humans hear from about twenty to twenty thousand hertz, while dogs and bats hear higher sounds.

beats.scene: Kofi shouts toward an old stone bridge across the river and listens
beats.summary: An echo is reflected sound, and the delay tells us how far away the reflecting wall is.

beats.scene: A bat and a ship with curved lines of sound ahead
beats.summary: Bats, ships and doctors use echoes, which is called echolocation or sonar.

beats.scene: Ama on a playground swing with Kofi giving her a small push each time
beats.summary: Resonance is when small pushes at the right rhythm make a big motion.

beats.scene: A crowd with hands over their ears at a concert beside a quiet library
beats.summary: Loud sounds carry more energy, and very loud ones can damage hearing, so ears need protection.

beats.scene: A beam of low sunlight crosses the misty riverbank between trees
beats.summary: Light is a wave that travels extremely fast, about three hundred thousand kilometres a second.

beats.scene: The still pond shows a mirror picture of the trees and sky
beats.summary: Light travels in straight lines, and a smooth surface reflects it at the same angle, as in a mirror.

beats.scene: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent
beats.summary: Light bends when it passes from air into water, which is called refraction.

beats.scene: Rain falls in low sunlight and a rainbow arches over the town
beats.summary: White light is a mix of colours that a prism or raindrops can separate.

beats.scene: A red sunset sky over the river with a bright blue sky overhead
beats.summary: The sky is blue and the sunset is red because air scatters blue light more than red.

beats.scene: A ladder of waves from radio to gamma rays, with a small rainbow
beats.summary: Visible light is one small part of a family of waves that also includes radio, infrared, ultraviolet and X-rays.

beats.scene: A television remote glowing in a phone camera and a bottle of sunscreen
beats.summary: Infrared carries heat and runs remote controls, while ultraviolet causes sunburn.

beats.scene: A glass lens bends a beam of light beside a boy in glasses
beats.summary: Lenses bend light, and this is how eyes, glasses and cameras work.

beats.scene: A drawing of an eye with light entering the lens
beats.summary: The eye's lens focuses light onto the retina, but the eye sees only a small part of the spectrum.

beats.scene: The last orange light on the river as the first star appears
beats.summary: Light, like sound, is a wave; but light is also linked to electricity, which comes next.

beats.scene: Kofi rubs a balloon on his hair and the hair stands up
beats.summary: Rubbing can move electric charge, and charges attract or repel.

beats.scene: A plus sign and a minus sign each drawn in a small circle
beats.summary: There are two kinds of electric charge, positive and negative, and rubbing moves some from one object to another.

beats.scene: Two balloons hang on strings and push apart, a third clings to the wall
beats.summary: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

beats.scene: A person in socks on a carpet reaching for a metal door handle
beats.summary: Static electricity builds up when you rub, and it jumps as a small shock when you touch metal.

beats.scene: A tiny atom drawn with a small negative electron circling a positive centre
beats.summary: Electrons carry negative charge and protons positive charge, and it is mostly the light electrons that move.

beats.scene: A copper wire and a rubber glove, with arrows moving along only the wire
beats.summary: Conductors such as metals let charge flow easily, while insulators such as rubber and plastic do not.

beats.scene: A dark storm cloud with ice crystals colliding inside it
beats.summary: Inside a storm cloud, colliding ice and water build up huge amounts of separated charge.

beats.scene: A huge bolt of lightning strikes a tall tree during a storm
beats.summary: Lightning is a giant spark of electric charge jumping between cloud and ground.

beats.scene: A tall house with a metal rod on its roof in a storm
beats.summary: A lightning rod gives lightning an easy path to the ground, an idea developed by Benjamin Franklin.

beats.scene: Three friends hurry up a path toward a house as raindrops fall
beats.summary: In a storm, shelter indoors or in a car, and stay away from tall trees and open ground.

beats.scene: The house goes dark in the storm and Zainab lights a torch
beats.summary: A power cut shows how much we rely on moving electric charge, and a battery torch still works.

beats.scene: A small lamp connected to a battery by a wire in a loop
beats.summary: Moving charges make a current, which flows when a battery pushes them round a circuit.

beats.scene: A torch taken apart on a table: battery, spring, bulb, switch
beats.summary: A torch is a simple circuit: battery, wires, switch and bulb in one loop.

beats.scene: A water pipe drawn beside a wire with a narrow part
beats.summary: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance holds the flow back.

beats.scene: A battery marked one and a half volts beside a wall socket
beats.summary: A torch battery gives about one and a half volts, while the mains is far stronger and dangerous.

beats.scene: A meter dial with a needle beside a kettle
beats.summary: Current is measured in amps; a strong kettle draws about nine amps from the mains.

beats.scene: A thick wire and a thin wire connected to the same battery
beats.summary: Resistance is measured in ohms, and a thin or long wire resists the current more than a thick or short one.

beats.scene: Two dim bulbs in a row beside two bright bulbs on branches
beats.summary: Bulbs in a row share the voltage and glow dimly, while bulbs on separate branches each get the full voltage.

beats.scene: A battery cut in half to show its layers
beats.summary: A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy, and a rechargeable one can be refilled.

beats.scene: Kitchen lights flicker back on beside a glowing toaster
beats.summary: Current heats a wire, which is how toasters work, and why a fuse melts to stop too much current.

beats.scene: Kofi holds two small magnets that pull together and push apart
beats.summary: Magnets have two poles; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

beats.scene: Iron filings in a pattern of curved lines around a bar magnet
beats.summary: A magnet is surrounded by a magnetic field, which acts on iron, nickel and cobalt.

beats.scene: A compass needle pointing north beside a drawing of the Earth with field lines
beats.summary: The Earth is a giant magnet, and a compass needle lines up with its field.

beats.scene: A compass needle swings away from a wire connected to a battery
beats.summary: An electric current makes a magnetic field, which was discovered by Hans Christian Oersted in 1820.

beats.scene: A coil of wire around a nail picks up pins
beats.summary: An electric current in a coil makes a magnetic field, as in an electromagnet.

beats.scene: A crane lifting a car with a round electromagnet above a scrapyard
beats.summary: Electromagnets can be switched on and off, and are used in cranes, bells and scanners.

beats.scene: A small electric motor spinning a fan between two magnets
beats.summary: A current in a magnetic field feels a force, which is how an electric motor turns.

beats.scene: A magnet moves in and out of a coil connected to a lamp
beats.summary: A moving magnet makes a current, which is how generators work.

beats.scene: A power station with a huge turbine, a wind farm, and a bicycle dynamo
beats.summary: Generators spin magnets inside coils, driven by steam, wind or water, and they supply the electricity we use.

beats.scene: A radio, a phone, and the glowing sun linked by wavy lines
beats.summary: Electricity, magnetism and light are one subject, electromagnetism, with light as a wave of both.

beats.scene: A night garden under clearing clouds, with a water drop in close-up
beats.summary: Everything is made of atoms, which are far too small to see.

beats.scene: Pollen grains dancing in a drop of water under a microscope
beats.summary: The jiggling of tiny grains in water is evidence for atoms, explained by Einstein in 1905.

beats.scene: A single human hair beside a row of tiny dots stretching across its width
beats.summary: A hair is about half a million atoms wide, and a drop of water holds an unimaginable number.

beats.scene: A huge empty stadium with a tiny grain of sand at its centre
beats.summary: An atom is mostly empty space with a tiny nucleus at its centre.

beats.scene: A nucleus of red and grey balls with small blue dots circling it
beats.summary: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, and the electrons around it are far lighter.

beats.scene: A wall chart of coloured squares beside a pile of different kinds of rock
beats.summary: There are about one hundred and eighteen kinds of atom, called elements.

beats.scene: A boy breathes out a cloud in the cold night garden
beats.summary: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, so each breath is a gulp of atoms that are billions of years old.

beats.scene: Two hydrogen atoms share electrons with an oxygen atom to make water
beats.summary: Atoms join by sharing or swapping their outer electrons to form molecules such as water.

beats.scene: A copper wire with a sea of glowing dots between its atoms
beats.summary: Metals conduct electricity because some of their electrons are free to move, while in insulators they are held tightly.

beats.scene: Rows of glowing blobs on a metal surface in an enlarged image
beats.summary: Special microscopes can now show individual atoms, and in 1989 scientists spelled a name with them.

beats.scene: A nucleus trembles and a small particle shoots out from it
beats.summary: Some nuclei are unstable and break apart, giving off radiation; this is radioactivity.

beats.scene: A woman in a laboratory beside glowing glass tubes and a notebook
beats.summary: Marie Curie studied radioactivity and won two Nobel Prizes, in physics and in chemistry.

beats.scene: Three arrows of different strengths stopped by paper, thin metal and thick lead
beats.summary: There are three main kinds of radiation, called alpha, beta and gamma, and they are stopped by different materials.

beats.scene: A dot-counting chart where half the dots fade after each equal step in time
beats.summary: The half-life is the time it takes for half of a radioactive sample to decay, which is used to date old objects.

beats.scene: A banana, a granite rock and a Geiger counter that clicks softly
beats.summary: Natural radiation is all around us, from rocks, food and space, in small and harmless amounts.

beats.scene: A big nucleus is hit and splits into two, with particles flying out
beats.summary: In fission, a heavy nucleus splits and releases energy and neutrons, which can start a chain reaction.

beats.scene: A nuclear power station with a cooling tower and a line of power cables
beats.summary: A nuclear power station uses controlled fission to boil water, drive a turbine and make electricity.

beats.scene: A tiny lump of mass beside a huge fireball, with a balance between them
beats.summary: Einstein's equation says that mass and energy are linked, so a little mass can become a huge amount of energy.

beats.scene: The Sun glows with arrows of hydrogen atoms joining into helium
beats.summary: In fusion, light nuclei join to make a heavier one and release energy; this is what powers the Sun.

beats.scene: A giant doughnut-shaped machine glowing purple inside a laboratory hall
beats.summary: Scientists are trying to build fusion reactors to copy the Sun, but it is very hard and not yet a power source.

beats.scene: A glowing packet of light hits metal and knocks out an electron
beats.summary: Quantum physics says that light and energy come in small packets called photons.

beats.scene: A staircase beside a smooth ramp, with a tiny ball on each
beats.summary: Energy in the tiny world comes in steps, called quanta, like stairs and not like a ramp.

beats.scene: A neon sign, a firework and a flame showing different bright colours
beats.summary: Atoms give off light of particular colours when electrons drop from one energy step to a lower one.

beats.scene: Electrons pass two narrow slits and make stripes on a screen
beats.summary: Light and even electrons can behave like waves and like particles, depending on how we look.

beats.scene: A thin beam of electrons passing through a microscope onto a tiny virus
beats.summary: Because electrons behave like waves with very short wavelengths, electron microscopes can see far smaller things than light can.

beats.scene: A tiny ball drawn as a blurred cloud in a box
beats.summary: Very small things behave in odd ways, and we can only know the odds of what they do.

beats.scene: Two identical atoms, one of which has decayed and one which has not
beats.summary: In the quantum world only probabilities can be predicted, as with the decay of a radioactive atom.

beats.scene: A small ball passes through a thin wall, with a bright star behind
beats.summary: Quantum tunnelling lets particles cross barriers that they should not be able to cross, and it helps the Sun to shine.

beats.scene: A computer chip beside a laser beam and a small phone
beats.summary: Quantum rules are tested and used in everyday devices such as chips, lasers and solar panels.

beats.scene: Kofi holds his phone showing a map under the dark sky
beats.summary: A phone holds billions of tiny switches and depends on atomic clocks in satellites, all built on quantum ideas.

beats.scene: Kofi and Zainab climb a dark hill behind the house with a blanket
beats.summary: After the storm, they climb the hill to look at the night sky.

beats.scene: A line of stars with a dotted path of light stretching back to them
beats.summary: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, and star light left them long ago.

beats.scene: A bright star with arrows pushing outward and arrows of gravity pushing inward
beats.summary: A star is held in balance between the inward pull of gravity and the outward push of heat from fusion.

beats.scene: A red star and a blue-white star shine side by side
beats.summary: Hot stars look blue-white and cooler stars look red, which uses the same idea as glowing metal.

beats.scene: A steady bright light low in the sky beside twinkling stars
beats.summary: Planets orbit the Sun because gravity keeps them falling around it, and they shine by reflected sunlight.

beats.scene: A boy holds out a hand that glows with tiny stars and atoms
beats.summary: Most of the atoms in our bodies, apart from hydrogen, were made inside stars long ago.

beats.scene: A pale glowing smudge in the dark sky beside a spiral galaxy drawing
beats.summary: Our Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, and other galaxies lie far beyond it.

beats.scene: A dark sky full of stars, with a few question marks floating among them
beats.summary: The universe is about thirteen point eight billion years old and is still expanding, and much remains unknown.

beats.scene: Kofi's notebook with all six lines on the envelope crossed off
beats.summary: The six ideas are crossed off, and Kofi sees that physics is for everyone.

beats.scene: Kofi and Zainab lie on a hill and look at the stars together
beats.summary: The six ideas explain an ordinary day and the stars above.

A1A2: Kofi asks his aunt what physics is, and she smiles.
Zainab writes six short words on the back of an old envelope.
Kofi says he is only twelve, and the list looks hard.
Zainab drops a spoon and asks Kofi why it falls.
Kofi measures the table with a tape and finds it is two metres long.
Kofi rolls an orange and times it with a stopwatch.
If an experiment disagrees with an idea, the idea must change.
Zainab says that even breakfast is full of physics.
Zainab packs a bag with a notebook, a magnet and a balloon.
They go outside, and the bicycle waits in the morning sun.
A bicycle stays still until someone pushes it.
Kofi gives the bike a push, and it rolls on and on.
Zainab flicks the card away, and the coin drops into the glass.
A car stops fast, and the things inside it move forward.
Kofi cycles past two trees, and Zainab times him.
Kofi and Ama go at the same speed, but in opposite directions.
Kofi starts slowly and pedals faster and faster.
Kofi rides round a bend and his direction changes.
Kofi gets faster by one metre per second, every second.
A force is a push or a pull that changes how things move.
Kofi pushes an empty cart easily, but a full cart is hard.
A hard push makes the cart go faster than a gentle push.
Zainab writes a short rule for forces on a paper bag.
A push of twenty newtons moves a ten kilogram box quickly.
A kick sends a light ball far, but a heavy ball hardly moves.
Two teams pull on a rope, but it does not move.
One team slips, and now the rope moves toward the other team.
Kofi pushes the wall, and his skateboard rolls away from it.
Air rushes out of the balloon, and the balloon shoots forward.
A rocket pushes hot gas down, and the gas pushes it up.
The brakes rub on the wheels and slow the bike down.
Friction helps us walk, because our shoes grip the ground.
Kofi rubs his hands together, and they feel warm.
An apple falls from the tree because the Earth pulls it.
Kofi drops a heavy ball and a light ball, and both fall together.
A feather falls slowly because the air holds it back.
A falling stone goes faster and faster as it falls.
A parachute catches the air and slows the person falling.
The Moon is always falling around the Earth, but it never lands.
Kofi would weigh less on the Moon, but his mass would stay.
At noon Kofi is hungry, and Zainab starts the second big idea.
Energy comes as movement, heat, light, sound, and more.
Fast things have more energy of movement than slow things.
If a car doubles its speed, it has four times the energy.
A big lorry has more energy than a bike at the same speed.
A roller coaster car at the top has stored energy.
Kofi pushes his bike up the hill, and he feels very tired.
A stretched rubber band stores energy and can shoot a paper ball.
Energy is counted in joules, and a small apple needs one joule.
At the top of the hill, Kofi looks down at the long road.
Kofi rolls down the hill without pedalling, and he goes fast.
A stone on a string swings up and down from side to side.
Energy changes from one form to another, but the total stays the same.
The stone swings less and less, and finally it stops.
On a roller coaster, the first hill is always the highest.
A ball bounces lower each time, and finally it lies still.
No machine can make energy from nothing, and many people have tried.
When Kofi pedals, a small lamp on his bike lights up.
A marble hits a line of marbles, and the last one shoots away.
Zainab says energy is like money that you can move around.
Kofi eats a sandwich, and the food gives him energy.
One sandwich holds more than a million joules of energy.
Kofi gives off as much heat as a bright light bulb.
A kettle uses much more power than a small light.
A bulb on for ten hours uses more than a kettle for one minute.
Petrol, coal, and gas hold energy that came from the Sun long ago.
Plants use sunlight to make their food, and animals eat plants.
Wind and solar panels also get their energy from the Sun.
Some energy does not come from the Sun, such as the tides.
A modern bulb gives the same light and uses less energy.
In the kitchen a kettle boils, and Zainab starts the third idea.
Ink spreads quickly in hot water and slowly in cold water.
A cup of hot tea is hotter than a bath of cool water.
Water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees.
A kettle takes about three minutes to boil a litre of water.
In the sun the sand gets hot quickly, but the sea stays cool.
Ice, water and steam are all made of the same molecules.
Ice in a drink stays cold until all of it has melted.
On a high mountain, water boils at a lower temperature.
When water dries from your skin, it takes heat away.
The hot tea warms the spoon, and the tea slowly cools.
A metal table feels colder than a wooden one in the same room.
Heat moves along a metal pan from molecule to molecule.
A wool jumper keeps you warm because it slows heat leaving.
A hot air balloon rises because warm air is lighter than cool air.
A radiator warms the air, and the warm air moves round the room.
The Sun's heat reaches us across empty space, as invisible rays.
A black shirt gets hotter in the sun than a white shirt.
A hot cup of tea slowly cools until it is as cool as the room.
The coldest possible place is minus 273 degrees Celsius.
Milk goes into coffee, and it never comes out again.
A tidy room gets messy by itself, but it never tidies itself.
Shuffled cards almost never come out in perfect order.
Heat spreads out, and spread out heat can do much less work.
An engine cannot turn all of its heat into movement.
Most of the energy in petrol becomes heat, not movement.
A fridge takes heat from the inside and sends it to the kitchen.
A cup breaks on the floor, but pieces never join back together.
Plants and people build order, but they need energy to do it.
Heat flows from hot to cold, and the world gets more mixed up.
Kofi drops a stone in the pond, and ripples spread.
Ama shakes a rope, and a bump runs along it to Kofi.
A spring toy shows a wave of pushing and pulling.
Zainab draws a wavy line and gives names to its parts.
Two ripples pass Kofi every second, so the frequency is two.
Some waves in the ocean are as fast as a jet plane.
Two sets of ripples cross, and neither one disappears.
The ripples hit the wall of the pond and bounce back.
Ripples go through a small gap and spread out on the other side.
Waves from earthquakes travel through the whole Earth.
Kofi sees lightning far away and counts the seconds until thunder.
Kofi hums with his hand on his throat and feels it buzz.
A bell in a jar with no air makes no sound at all.
Sound travels faster in metal than it does in the air.
A short string makes a high note, and a long string makes a low note.
Dogs can hear high sounds that people cannot hear.
Kofi shouts at the bridge, and his voice comes back later.
Bats and ships send out sounds, and they listen for echoes.
Kofi pushes Ama's swing at just the right time, and she goes high.
Very loud sounds can hurt your ears, so you should protect them.
Light is a wave that travels faster than anything else.
The calm pond works like a mirror and shows the trees.
A pencil in a glass of water looks bent.
A rainbow shows all the colours that are hidden in sunlight.
The sky is blue, but sunsets are red, and air makes the difference.
Light is only one kind in a big family of waves.
Infrared rays carry heat, and ultraviolet rays can burn your skin.
A lens bends light, and glasses use lenses to help people see.
Your eye has a lens that puts a picture at the back.
The sun goes down, and the fourth idea is finished.
Kofi rubs a balloon on his hair, and his hair stands up.
There are two kinds of charge, called positive and negative.
Two charged balloons push each other apart, but one sticks to the wall.
After walking on a carpet, Kofi gets a small shock from a door.
Tiny electrons carry negative charge, and they can move from place to place.
Metals let charge move easily, but rubber and plastic do not.
In a storm cloud, ice and water rub together and make charge.
Lightning is a huge spark that jumps from a cloud to the ground.
A metal rod on a roof lets lightning go safely to the ground.
The storm comes closer, and they run home before the rain.
The storm cuts the power, and Zainab finds a torch.
A battery pushes tiny electrons round a wire and lights a lamp.
Kofi opens the torch and finds a battery, a switch and a bulb.
Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance holds it back.
A torch battery is safe to touch, but a wall socket is not.
Current is counted in amps, and a kettle uses nine of them.
A thin wire makes it harder for current to flow than a thick wire.
Two bulbs in a row are dim, but separate bulbs are bright.
A battery uses chemicals to make power for the lamp.
The lights come on again, and the toaster wires glow orange.
Two magnets pull together one way and push apart the other way.
Iron dust shows the invisible lines around a magnet.
A compass needle always points north, because the Earth is a magnet.
When a current flows, a compass needle near the wire moves.
A wire around a nail picks up pins when the battery is on.
Big cranes use electromagnets to lift old cars.
A motor uses magnets and current to turn a fan.
A moving magnet near a coil of wire makes electricity.
Power stations spin big magnets inside coils to make electricity.
Light, radio and electricity are all parts of one big idea.
After the storm, the garden shines, and Zainab starts the sixth idea.
Small dots in water dance about, because atoms keep hitting them.
A hair is about half a million atoms wide.
An atom is mostly empty, with a tiny nucleus in the middle.
The nucleus has protons and neutrons, and electrons are outside.
There are about one hundred and eighteen kinds of atom.
Each breath of air is full of atoms of nitrogen and oxygen.
Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom join to make water.
Some electrons in a metal can move, so power can flow.
Today special microscopes can show pictures of single atoms.
Some atoms are unstable, and they give off energy as they change.
Marie Curie studied strange rays and won two big prizes.
Different kinds of radiation need different things to stop them.
A half-life is the time for half the atoms to decay.
A little natural radiation is all around us, even in food.
A heavy nucleus can split into two, and it gives out a lot of energy.
A nuclear power station makes heat from splitting atoms.
Mass can become energy, and a tiny mass makes a huge amount.
The Sun joins small nuclei together, and this gives out energy.
Scientists try to make a small Sun on the Earth.
Light comes in tiny packets, and each packet is called a photon.
In the tiny world, energy comes in steps, like stairs.
Each kind of atom gives off its own special colours of light.
Tiny things such as electrons can act like waves.
An electron microscope uses electron waves to see very small things.
At the smallest size, nature is always a little blurry.
We can say how likely something is, but not what will happen.
A tiny particle can sometimes pass through a barrier it should not.
Chips, lasers, and phones all use the strange rules of quantum physics.
A phone has billions of tiny switches, called transistors, inside it.
After the storm, they climb the hill with a blanket.
The light from the stars left them a very long time ago.
A star is a huge Sun, held together by its own gravity.
Hot stars look blue and cool stars look red.
One bright light does not blink, because it is a planet.
The atoms in your body were made inside stars long ago.
The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in our galaxy.
The universe is very old, and there is much we still do not know.
Kofi crosses off the last line on the envelope.
They lie on the hill, and the stars shine above them.
B1B2: Kofi thinks physics is only for scientists in white coats. His aunt Zainab laughs and says that six big ideas can explain his whole day.
Zainab takes an envelope and writes six headings on it. They are motion and forces, energy, heat, waves, electricity and magnetism, and atoms.
Kofi worries that the list looks far too difficult for a boy of twelve. Zainab tells him that physics always begins with simple questions, and he is already good at asking them.
Zainab lets a spoon fall and asks Kofi why it does not float away. She says that physics means asking why things happen and then testing the answer.
Physics depends on careful measuring, so scientists agree on units. The metre measures length, the second measures time, and the kilogram measures mass.
Kofi rolls an orange along the table and times it with a stopwatch. When Zainab divides the distance by the time, she gets a number for its speed.
Zainab says that every idea in physics must agree with experiments. If an experiment disagrees with it, the idea has to change, however famous the person who suggested it.
Zainab points around the table and says that breakfast is already full of physics. The moving spoon, the warm toast, the crunch and the humming toaster belong to her six ideas.
Zainab packs a rucksack for the day with a notebook, a stopwatch, a small magnet and a balloon. She says that a few simple tools are enough to find out a great deal.
The two of them step outside into the cool morning air. Kofi's bicycle is leaning against the wall, and Zainab says that the first idea begins right there.
A parked bicycle will stay exactly where it is for ever, unless something pushes it. Zainab says this is the first great rule of motion.
Kofi gives the bicycle a strong push and lets go. It rolls a long way down the road before it slowly comes to a stop.
Zainab balances a coin on a card over a glass, then flicks the card away. The coin does not fly off with it, but drops straight down into the glass.
When a car brakes suddenly, everything inside tends to keep moving forward. This is why seat belts are so important, because they hold passengers back.
Kofi cycles along the road while Zainab times him between two trees that are fifty metres apart. He takes ten seconds, so his speed is about five metres every second.
Ama rides toward Kofi at the same speed as he rides toward her. Zainab says their speeds are equal, but their velocities are not, because velocity includes direction.
Kofi starts from a standstill and pedals harder, going faster every second. Zainab says that any change in velocity is called acceleration.
Kofi rides round a bend without changing his speed. Zainab says he is still accelerating, because his direction is changing, and velocity includes direction.
Kofi speeds up from zero to five metres per second in five seconds. That is a gain of one metre per second, every second, and this is his acceleration.
A force is a push or a pull, and it is measured in units called newtons. Zainab says that a force is the only thing that can change how an object moves.
Outside Mr Boateng's shop, Kofi pushes an empty cart and then a cart full of tins. The empty one speeds up quickly, but the full one hardly moves.
Kofi pushes the same empty cart gently and then very hard. The harder push makes it speed up much faster, so more force gives more acceleration.
Zainab writes a short rule on a paper bag: force equals mass times acceleration. She says the whole of Newton's second law is in those few words.
A box has a mass of ten kilograms, and Kofi pushes it with a force of twenty newtons. Dividing the force by the mass shows that it speeds up by two metres per second, every second.
Ama kicks a light tennis ball and then a heavy ball of the same size. The light ball flies away, but the heavy one rolls only a short way.
At the school field two teams are playing tug of war, and they pull with equal strength. The rope stays still, because the two forces cancel each other out.
Suddenly one team slips on the damp grass and its pull gets weaker. Now the net force is not zero, and the rope speeds up toward the stronger team.
On Ama's skateboard Kofi pushes against a wall and rolls backward. Zainab says that when he pushes the wall, the wall pushes him back just as hard.
Zainab ties a string across the garden and lets go of a blown-up balloon. As the air rushes backward out of it, the balloon is pushed forward along the string.
A rocket throws hot gas out of its engines at great speed, and the gas pushes the rocket the other way. It works even in space, where there is no air to push against.
When two surfaces rub together, a force called friction pushes against the movement. The brakes use friction to stop the bike, and they get warm because the movement is turned into heat.
Friction is not only a nuisance, because without it we could not walk. Our shoes grip the ground, and a wet floor is slippery because it has less friction.
Kofi rubs his hands together quickly and holds them against his cheeks. They feel warm because friction turns the movement of the skin into heat.
An apple falls from a branch and lands near Kofi's feet. A famous story says that watching an apple helped Newton to think about gravity, which pulls everything toward the Earth.
Kofi drops a heavy ball and a light ball together from a wall. To his surprise, they land at the same moment, as Galileo found about four hundred years ago.
A feather falls much more slowly than a stone, but only because the air slows it. In 1971 an astronaut on the Moon dropped a feather and a hammer, and they landed together.
A falling stone speeds up all the time as it falls toward the ground. Near the Earth it gains about ten metres per second of speed, every second, so after three seconds it is going about thirty.
As something falls faster, the air pushes back harder. A parachute is wide, so it catches a lot of air, and the person lands gently.
Kofi sees the Moon in the daytime sky and asks why it does not fall down. Zainab says it does fall, but it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the Earth.
Mass is the amount of matter in something, and weight is the pull of gravity on it. On the Moon Kofi would weigh about six times less, but his mass would be the same.
By noon Kofi is hungry, so they sit down in the park, and Zainab begins the second big idea. Energy, she says, is the ability to make something change or to make something happen.
Energy shows itself in many forms, such as movement, heat, light and sound. It can also be stored, in a battery, in food, in a stretched spring or in a high place.
Energy of movement is called kinetic energy, and it depends on the mass and on the speed. A fast cyclist has much more of it than a slow one.
If you double the speed, the kinetic energy becomes four times greater, because speed counts twice in the sum. A car at sixty kilometres an hour carries four times the energy of one at thirty.
A heavy lorry and a bicycle move at the same speed along the road. The lorry has far more kinetic energy because its mass is bigger, so it takes much longer to stop.
Ama says that a roller coaster car at the top of its track is full of stored energy. The word for this is potential energy, and it can turn into movement as soon as the car starts to fall.
After lunch Kofi pushes his bicycle up the hill, and the climb makes him tired. It takes a lot of energy to lift himself and the bicycle higher, and that energy is stored in the height.
Zainab stretches a rubber band, and it stores energy as it is pulled. When she lets go, the energy is released and the band shoots a ball of paper into the air.
Energy is measured in units called joules, after a scientist named James Joule. Lifting a small apple up by one metre takes about one joule, and the climb up the hill took Kofi tens of thousands.
At last Kofi reaches the top, and the whole town lies spread out below. The bicycle now holds a great deal of stored energy, and the long road down is waiting.
Kofi lets the bicycle roll down the hill without pedalling. As he drops, the stored energy of height turns into energy of movement, and he goes faster and faster.
Zainab hangs a stone on a string from a branch and lets it swing. At the high points the stone is still for an instant, and at the low point it moves the fastest.
Zainab says that energy is never made and never destroyed. It only changes from one form to another, and the total always stays the same.
Kofi notices that the stone swings lower and lower, until it hangs still. The air and the branch have made a little heat from its energy, so none of the energy has really been lost.
On a roller coaster, the first hill is nearly always the tallest. Ama explains that the car loses a little energy as heat all the way round, so it cannot climb as high again.
Kofi drops a ball on the path and counts the bounces. Each bounce is lower than the one before, because some of the energy turns into heat and sound every time it hits the ground.
For hundreds of years, inventors have tried to build a machine that runs for ever without fuel. None has worked, because that would mean creating energy from nothing, and the law forbids it.
Kofi's bicycle has a small lamp that lights while the wheel turns. His leg energy becomes movement, and then the movement becomes light and a little heat.
Ama rolls a marble into a row of marbles that are touching. The energy passes along the row, and the marble at the far end shoots away.
Zainab says that energy is like money in a bank. You can move it between accounts and change it into other kinds of money, but you cannot make more of it out of nothing.
Back at the bench Kofi eats a second sandwich. Food holds chemical energy, which the body uses to move its muscles and to stay warm.
Zainab says that one sandwich holds well over a million joules of energy. That is a huge number, but the body uses it up in only a few hours.
A person who is sitting still gives off heat at about the rate of an old bright light bulb. Zainab says it is roughly one hundred watts, so Kofi is a warm boy.
Power is how fast energy is used, and it is measured in watts. A small light bulb may use about ten watts, while an electric kettle may use two or three thousand.
The energy a machine uses depends on its power and on how long it runs. A kettle uses a lot of power, but only for a few minutes, so a light left on all night may use more.

Coal, oil and gas are called fossil fuels, and they formed from ancient living things. They took millions of years to form from the remains of plants and tiny sea animals, so they hold sunlight from long ago.
Plants catch sunlight with their green leaves and use it to make food from air and water. Animals and people then eat the plants, so the energy of nearly all food came from the Sun.
Wind turbines and solar panels give us energy that comes from the Sun. The Sun warms the air unevenly, which makes the wind, and it lifts water into clouds, which fills the rivers.
A few sources of energy do not come from the Sun. The tides are caused by the pull of the Moon, and deep inside the Earth there is heat that can warm water.
A modern light bulb gives as much light as an old one while using far less energy. Choosing efficient machines and switching things off are easy ways to waste less.
In the afternoon they return to Zainab's kitchen, where the kettle is boiling. Heat, she says, is the third big idea, and it is really about the movement of tiny molecules.
Zainab puts a drop of ink in a glass of hot water and another in a glass of cold water. The ink spreads far faster in the hot water, because the molecules there are moving faster.
Temperature tells us how fast the molecules are moving on average. A bath of cool water holds much more heat than a cup of hot tea, because it has so many more molecules.
On the Celsius scale, water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred, when it is measured at sea level. A healthy person's body stays at about thirty-seven degrees.
Warming one litre of water from a cool temperature to boiling takes roughly three hundred and fifty thousand joules. A strong kettle can supply that in about three minutes.
On a sunny day the sand on a beach gets too hot to walk on, while the sea stays cool. Water takes a great deal of energy to warm up, much more than sand does.

A block of ice, a glass of water and a cloud of steam are made of exactly the same molecules. In ice they are locked in place, in water they slide past one another, and in steam they fly about freely.
Ice cubes in a drink stay at zero degrees until every bit has melted. While they melt they soak up a great deal of heat from the drink, which is why they cool it so well.
High on a mountain, the air presses less on the water, so it boils at a lower temperature. Climbers find that tea made up there is only just hot, and it takes longer to cook food.
When water evaporates from your skin it takes heat away, and you feel cooler. This is how sweating protects the body in hot weather, and why blowing on tea cools it.
Kofi leaves a metal spoon in his hot tea, and soon the handle feels warm. Heat always flows from a hot thing to a colder thing, and never the other way round by itself.
A metal table leg feels colder than a wooden chair leg, although both are at the same room temperature. Metal carries heat away from your hand much faster than wood does.
Heat moves through a solid by a process called conduction. The hot molecules shake faster and knock against their neighbours, passing the energy along, which is why the handle of a pan gets hot.
A woollen jumper keeps you warm because it traps air, and air conducts heat very badly. A vacuum flask keeps tea hot for hours for the same sort of reason.
Warm air spreads out, so it is lighter than the cooler air around it, and it rises. A hot air balloon uses this, and the rising and sinking of air is called convection.
A radiator warms the air beside it, and the warm air rises to the ceiling. Cooler air then sinks and flows toward the radiator, and this circle spreads the heat around the whole room.
Heat can also travel as invisible rays, which is called radiation. The Sun warms us this way across about one hundred and fifty million kilometres of empty space.
A black shirt hung in the sun gets hotter than a white one. Dark surfaces take in radiation, while pale and shiny surfaces reflect much of it away.
A cup of hot tea will cool down until it is exactly as warm as the room around it. At that point the heat stops flowing, and scientists say the two are in thermal equilibrium.
There is a lowest temperature, called absolute zero, at about minus 273 degrees Celsius. At that point the molecules have as little energy as they can have, so nothing can be colder.
Kofi pours milk into Zainab's coffee, and it swirls and spreads until the whole cup is brown. Stirring the other way will never make the milk separate again.
A tidy room becomes messy by itself, but a messy room never tidies itself. There are far more ways for things to be messy than tidy, so mess is much more likely.
A shuffled pack of cards almost never comes out in perfect order. Scientists call the amount of disorder entropy, and the second law says that in a closed system it tends to increase.
When a hot cup cools, its energy spreads into the room. Spread-out energy is much less useful, because a warm room cannot boil anything.
A car engine burns fuel to make heat, and it turns some of that heat into movement. It can never turn all of it, and the rest has to flow away into the cooler air.
A petrol car uses only about a quarter to a third of the energy in its fuel to move. The rest leaves as hot gas and warm metal, and this is why electric motors are much more efficient.
A fridge moves heat from its cold inside to the warmer kitchen, which is the opposite of the natural direction. It needs electricity to do this, and the back of it is always warm.
A cup that falls off a table breaks into pieces, but broken pieces never jump back together. If you saw that on a film, you would know that the film was running backward.
A living thing is very ordered, and it seems to go against the second law. But plants and people need a steady supply of energy, and they give out heat, so the total disorder still grows.
Zainab crosses the third idea off the envelope, saying that heat flows from hot to cold and the world drifts toward disorder. Then they walk to the river, where the fourth idea is waiting.
Zainab's fourth idea is the wave, which is a disturbance that travels and carries energy from place to place. The ripples move across the pond, but the water does not travel with them.
Ama holds one end of a long rope and Kofi holds the other. When she shakes her end, a wave runs along the rope to him, but the rope itself stays where it is.
Ama pushes one end of a spring toy and a squeezed patch runs along it. This kind of wave, in which the coils move forward and back, is called a longitudinal wave.
Zainab draws a wavy line in the damp sand and names its parts. The top is a crest, the bottom is a trough, and the distance from crest to crest is the wavelength.

The number of waves that pass a point in each second is called the frequency, and it is measured in hertz. If the ripples are ten centimetres apart and two pass each second, they move at twenty centimetres per second.
Some waves in the ocean can travel extremely fast. A tsunami, which is caused by an earthquake under the sea, can cross a deep ocean at around eight hundred kilometres an hour.
Kofi drops two stones into the pond a short distance apart. The two sets of ripples cross each other and make a pattern, and then each one carries on as though the other were not there.
When the ripples reach the stone edge of the pond, they bounce back toward the middle. Waves bounce off hard surfaces, and this is called reflection.
Ama builds two low walls with a small gap in the sand, and the ripples pass through it. On the far side they spread out in half circles, which is a wave's way of bending around corners.

Earthquakes send waves through the whole Earth, and scientists measure them with sensitive instruments. By studying how the waves travel, they have learned about the hot, deep layers that nobody can visit.
A storm is far away over the hills, and Kofi sees a flash of lightning. He counts the seconds until the thunder arrives, because light is almost instant, but sound travels much more slowly.
Kofi puts his fingers on his throat and hums, and he can feel a buzzing. All sounds are made by something that vibrates, and the vibrations travel through the air as waves.
Zainab says that if you ring a bell inside a jar and pump out the air, the sound fades away. Sound needs something to travel through, so in space nobody can hear you shout.
Ama taps the long metal railing with a stone, and Kofi puts his ear against the far end. He hears the tap twice, first through the metal and then through the air, because sound is faster in metal.
Pitch is how high or low a sound is, and it depends on the frequency of the vibration. A short, tight string vibrates faster and makes a higher note, while a hard pluck makes a louder sound.
Humans can hear sounds from about twenty to twenty thousand hertz. Dogs can hear higher sounds than people, so Biscuit hears a whistle that Kofi cannot, and bats hear even higher ones.
Kofi shouts toward the stone bridge, and half a second later his voice comes back. In half a second sound travels about one hundred and seventy metres, so the bridge is about eighty-five metres away.

A bat sends out high squeaks and listens for the echoes to find insects in the dark. Ships use the same idea, called sonar, to measure the depth of the sea, and doctors use ultrasound to look at babies.
Kofi pushes Ama's swing a little each time it comes back to him, and soon it is swinging very high. Small pushes at the right rhythm add up, and this is called resonance.
Loud sounds are waves with a lot of energy. A whisper is about thirty decibels and a concert is over one hundred, which can damage your hearing.
As the sun sinks, a beam of light shines through the mist by the river. Light is a wave that travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second, which is faster than anything else.
The calm surface of the pond shows a perfect picture of the trees. Light travels in straight lines, and a smooth surface sends it back at the same angle, which is how a mirror works.
Zainab puts a pencil in a glass of water, and it looks bent at the surface. Light slows down and changes direction when it passes from air into water, and this bending is called refraction.
Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of every colour, and each colour is a wave of a different length. Raindrops bend the colours by different amounts and spread them into a rainbow.
Air scatters the blue part of sunlight in every direction, so the sky looks blue. At sunset the light travels through much more air, so most of the blue is lost and the red is left.
Visible light is only one small part of a large family of waves. The family includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, which differ only in wavelength.
Infrared rays carry heat and are used in remote controls and night cameras. Ultraviolet rays from the Sun can burn the skin, so people should use sunscreen and wear a hat.
A lens is a curved piece of glass that bends light to a single point. Glasses, cameras, telescopes and even your eyes all use lenses to make a clear picture.
Your eye has a lens that focuses light into a small picture at the back, which is called the retina. Your eyes see only a small part of the spectrum, but bees can also see ultraviolet.
The sun goes down, and the fourth idea is finished. Zainab says that light is a wave of a surprising kind, because it is made of electricity and magnetism, which are her fifth idea.
On the way home Kofi rubs a balloon against his hair, and then the hairs rise up toward it. Zainab says this is the start of her fifth idea, which is electricity.
There are two kinds of electric charge, called positive and negative. Rubbing moves some of the negative charge from one thing to another, so one becomes positive and the other negative.
Zainab hangs two charged balloons from strings, and they swing away from each other. Charges that are the same push each other apart, while charges that are different pull together.
If you shuffle across a carpet in socks and then touch a metal door handle, you may get a small shock. The charge you collected jumps across in a tiny spark.

The charge that moves when we rub things is carried by electrons, which are tiny particles found in every atom. Protons carry the opposite charge, but they are heavy and stay in the middle of the atom.
Some materials let electric charge flow through them easily, and they are called conductors. Metals such as copper are good conductors, but rubber and plastic are insulators, which block the flow.
In a storm cloud, tiny pieces of ice and water are carried up and down by strong winds. Scientists think that they rub together and build up a huge amount of electric charge.

Lightning is a giant spark that jumps between the cloud and the ground. It heats the air around it to about thirty thousand degrees Celsius, and the air bursts outward with a bang that we hear as thunder.
In the eighteenth century Benjamin Franklin suggested that a metal rod on a roof could lead lightning safely to the ground. Many tall buildings still have lightning rods, and they save many lives.
The storm comes closer, so they hurry up the path to the house. In a thunderstorm the safest places are inside a building or a car, and not under a tall tree or in an open field.
A great crack of thunder shakes the house, and every light goes out. Zainab finds a torch in a drawer, and its little bulb lights up the kitchen at once.
An electric current is a flow of charge, usually electrons moving along a wire. A battery gives them a push, but they will only flow if there is a complete loop, called a circuit.
Kofi unscrews the torch and spreads its parts on the table. He finds a battery, a metal spring, a switch and a bulb, and Zainab shows how they make a single loop.
Zainab compares a wire to a water pipe, because the two ideas are alike. Voltage is the pressure, current is the amount of water flowing, and resistance is a narrow part of the pipe.
A torch battery gives about one and a half volts, which is perfectly safe to touch. The electricity in a wall socket is more than one hundred times stronger, and it can be very dangerous.
Current is measured in amperes, or amps for short. A kettle that uses two thousand watts from the mains draws about nine amps, while a small torch bulb needs only a fraction of one.
A thin wire makes it harder for the current to flow than a thick wire does. This hold-back is called resistance, and it is measured in units called ohms.

When two bulbs are connected in a row, they share the push of the battery and glow dimly. When they are on separate branches, each one gets the full push, and one can fail while the other keeps shining.
A battery has chemicals inside, and a chemical reaction pushes the charges along the wire. When the chemicals are used up the battery is flat, but a rechargeable battery can be filled again.
When the power comes back, Kofi makes toast and watches the wires glow. A current heats a wire, and a fuse in the plug is a thin wire that melts if the current gets too big.
Zainab takes the magnet from her rucksack and gives Kofi a second one. Each magnet has two poles, and like poles push each other away, while unlike poles pull together.
Zainab sprinkles iron filings on paper above a magnet, and they line up in curved lines. These lines show the magnetic field, which pulls on iron, nickel and cobalt but not on copper or wood.
A compass needle is a small magnet that turns to line up with the Earth's own magnetic field. The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, and the compass points toward its magnetic north.
Zainab puts a compass next to a wire and joins the wire to a battery. The needle swings, which shows that an electric current makes a magnetic field around it.
Zainab winds wire around a nail and joins the ends to a battery. The nail now behaves like a magnet and picks up small pins, because the current in the coil makes a magnetic field.
A big electromagnet is used in a scrapyard to lift old cars, and it is released by switching off the current. Electromagnets are also in doorbells, speakers and hospital scanners.
A wire carrying current feels a push in a magnetic field. In an electric motor this push keeps a coil turning, and the motor can spin a fan, a drill or a car.
Zainab moves a magnet in and out of a coil connected to a small lamp, and the lamp flickers. A changing magnetic field makes a current in the wire, which was discovered by Michael Faraday.
Power stations use huge generators in which magnets spin inside coils of wire. Steam, wind or falling water turns the generators, and your bicycle lamp uses a tiny version of the same idea.

A changing electric field makes a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. Together they travel as electromagnetic waves, which include light, radio and the signals for your phone.
The storm passes, and Kofi and Zainab step into the wet garden. The sixth idea, she says, is that everything, from the grass to the stars, is made of atoms too small to see.

In the 1820s a scientist saw tiny grains of pollen dancing in water. In 1905 Einstein showed that the dance was caused by unseen molecules bumping into the grains, and this helped to prove that atoms are real.
A single human hair is only about half a million atoms wide. A drop of water contains more atoms than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the world.
An atom has a tiny nucleus in the middle and a cloud of electrons around it. If the atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a grain of sand, and the rest would be almost empty.
The nucleus is made of protons, which have positive charge, and neutrons, which have no charge. The electrons, with negative charge, are far lighter and move around outside it.
There are about one hundred and eighteen kinds of atom, which are called elements. The number of protons in the nucleus decides which element an atom belongs to.
The air that Kofi breathes is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen. Every breath contains a vast number of atoms, and they have been recycled for billions of years.
Atoms join together by sharing their outer electrons, and a group of joined atoms is called a molecule. Water is made of one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms, which is why we write it as H two O.
In a metal, some electrons are free to wander between the atoms. This is why metals carry electricity so well, while in rubber and plastic the electrons are held tightly in place.
Today, special microscopes that feel a surface with a needle can make pictures of single atoms. In 1989 scientists even used thirty-five atoms of xenon to spell out the letters of their company.
The nuclei of some atoms are unstable, and they give off radiation as they change, which we call radioactivity. Zainab says that this is the most dramatic thing that atoms can do.
The Polish scientist Marie Curie studied radioactive materials more than a hundred years ago and gave radioactivity its name. She won two Nobel prizes, one in physics and one in chemistry.

Radioactive atoms give off three main kinds of radiation, which are called alpha, beta and gamma. A sheet of paper stops alpha, a thin sheet of metal stops beta, and gamma needs thick lead or concrete.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes for half of its atoms to change. Carbon fourteen has a half-life of about five thousand seven hundred years, so it can be used to date old wooden objects.
A small amount of natural radiation is all around us, in rocks, in food and from space. A banana contains a tiny amount of radioactive potassium, but the dose is far too small to harm anyone.

In fission, a neutron hits a heavy nucleus, such as uranium, and splits it into two smaller pieces. It releases a great deal of energy and more neutrons, which can split other nuclei in a chain reaction.

A nuclear power station uses controlled fission to make heat, which boils water into steam. The steam turns a turbine and a generator, and nuclear power gives about a tenth of the electricity in the world.
In 1905 Einstein found that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. His equation says that energy equals mass times the speed of light squared, so a tiny mass makes a huge amount of energy.
In fusion, two light nuclei join to make a heavier one and release energy. Deep in the Sun, hydrogen is fused into helium, and about four million tonnes of mass turns into energy every second.
Scientists are trying to copy the Sun on the Earth with fusion reactors, but it is very hard. The gas has to be heated to more than one hundred million degrees, and no reactor yet makes useful power.
Zainab says that at the smallest scale, light comes in tiny packets called photons. When one photon hits a piece of metal, it can knock an electron out, as Einstein explained in 1905.
On a ramp you can stand at any height, but on stairs you can only stand on the steps. In the world of atoms, energy comes in steps like stairs, and the word for one step is a quantum.
When an electron drops from a high step to a lower one, the atom gives off a photon of one exact colour. This is why neon signs and fireworks glow with their own special colours.
Zainab says that tiny things can act like waves and like particles at once. When electrons are sent through two narrow slits, they make a striped pattern on the screen, just as water waves do.
