The wave behaviour of electrons is also very useful in practice. An electron microscope uses waves that are much shorter than light, so it can show details thousands of times smaller than a normal microscope.
In 1927 Werner Heisenberg showed that we cannot know exactly where a tiny particle is and exactly how fast it moves at the same time. This is not a failing of our instruments, but a rule of nature.
Two identical radioactive atoms may decay at very different times, and nobody can say which will go first. Quantum physics can only tell us the odds, like a pair of dice that nobody can see.
A tiny particle can sometimes pass through a barrier that it should not have enough energy to cross. This is called tunnelling, and the Sun could not shine without it.
The strange rules of quantum physics are used in everyday devices. Computer chips, lasers, LED lights and solar panels all depend on them, and so do the scanners in hospitals.
Inside a modern phone are billions of transistors, which are tiny switches made from silicon. The map on the screen also depends on exact clocks in satellites that use the quantum steps of atoms.
The rain has stopped, so Kofi and Zainab climb the hill behind the house with a blanket. Away from the street lights, the sky is full of stars.

A light-year is the distance that light travels in a year, which is about nine and a half million million kilometres. The light from the stars has been travelling for years, so we see them as they were.

Every star is a huge Sun held together by its own gravity. Fusion in the middle makes heat that pushes outward, and this balances the inward pull, so the star can shine steadily for millions of years.
Zainab says that the colour of a star shows its temperature. The hottest stars look blue-white and the cooler ones look red, just as a heated piece of metal glows red and then white.
Zainab points to a steady bright light that does not twinkle, and says it is a planet. Planets shine only by reflecting sunlight, and they stay in orbit around the Sun by gravity.
The atoms in our bodies, apart from hydrogen, were made inside stars. When old stars exploded, they scattered the atoms into space, and later they became part of the Earth and of us.
Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in a galaxy called the Milky Way. Beyond it are billions of other galaxies, and from a dark place you can see the Andromeda galaxy with your own eyes.

The universe began about thirteen billion eight hundred million years ago, and it is still growing larger. There is much that physicists do not yet understand, and that is why physics is still exciting.
Kofi takes out the envelope and crosses off the last line with a pencil. He has met all six ideas in a single day, and he knows that physics is not only for scientists in white coats.

Kofi and Zainab lie on the blanket and watch the stars, and Kofi is already thinking of a question for tomorrow. The six ideas explain a bicycle ride, a cup of tea and a storm, and also the stars above.

His aunt Zainab, who taught the subject at the town school, laughed and said that just six big ideas could explain almost everything he would do that day. They agreed to take the ideas one at a time, beginning with the bicycle waiting outside.

Zainab turned over an envelope and wrote six headings down the back, in her neat teacher's handwriting. Motion and forces came first, followed by energy, heat, waves, electricity with magnetism, and finally the atoms from which everything is built. “Keep this in your pocket,” she said, “and by tonight you will be able to cross off every line.”

Kofi stared at the envelope and admitted that the list looked far too grand for a boy of only twelve. Zainab shook her head and explained that physics begins with exactly the kind of question a child asks, such as why a ball falls down instead of up. The great scientists, she added, were mostly people who never grew out of asking.

Zainab let a teaspoon slip from her fingers and asked Kofi why it dropped to the floor instead of drifting up to the ceiling. Before he could answer, she explained that physics is a habit of mind, in which we ask why something happens, suggest a reason, and then test that reason carefully. An idea that survives the test is kept, and one that fails is thrown away.

A question about the world is only half answered until we can put a number to it, which is why physicists measure everything carefully. They have agreed on shared units, so a metre is the same in every country, a second is the same on every clock, and a kilogram means the same amount of matter in every shop. Kofi's own breakfast table, when he stretched the tape along it, turned out to be almost exactly two metres long.

Kofi rolled an orange along the length of the table while Zainab pressed the button on her stopwatch, and the trip took about two seconds. Dividing the distance by the time gave them the orange's speed, and that single number was enough to predict how far it would travel in any other time. This power to predict is the reason why physics leans so heavily on mathematics.

Zainab told Kofi that the final judge in physics is never a famous name, a teacher or a textbook, but an experiment that anyone can repeat. If the careful measurements disagree with a beautiful idea, then the idea must be changed, even when its author is a genius. Kofi liked this rule, because it meant that a twelve-year-old with a good test could, in principle, be right.

Zainab swept her hand across the breakfast table and announced that every one of her six ideas was sitting there already. The spoon in motion, the energy in the cereal, the heat of the toast, the crunch that reached their ears and the electricity in the toaster all belonged on the envelope, and so did the atoms inside the milk. Kofi suddenly saw his ordinary breakfast, with its toast and tea and cereal, as a small and delicious laboratory.

While Kofi finished his cereal, Zainab filled a canvas rucksack with the equipment for the day, which included a notebook, a stopwatch, a small magnet, a balloon and a long piece of string. None of it was expensive or complicated, because she believed that a few simple tools and a curious mind could uncover a surprising amount. Kofi slung the bag over his shoulder, feeling rather like an explorer setting off to map an unknown country.

The front door opened onto a cool, bright morning, with dew still glittering on the grass and a few early birds calling from the hedge. Kofi's bicycle was leaning against the wall where he had left it the night before, looking perfectly ordinary and perfectly still. Zainab smiled and told him that the first of her six ideas, the one about motion and forces, was already hiding in that stillness.

Zainab pointed at the parked bicycle and asked Kofi how long it would stay there if nobody touched it. He guessed that it would wait for ever, and she told him that he had just stated the first great rule of motion. An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving in the same way, unless some force interferes.

Kofi gave the empty bicycle a firm shove and let go of the handlebars, and it rolled a surprisingly long way along the flat road. It did not stop because it wanted to rest, Zainab explained, but because friction and the air were quietly pushing against it all the time. Without those two quiet pushes working against it, the bicycle would have rolled on in a straight line for ever.

On a flat stone wall, Zainab balanced a card over a glass and placed a coin on top of the card. With one sharp flick she sent the card spinning away, and the coin, which had been sitting still, simply dropped into the glass. The coin's stubborn tendency to stay where it was is called inertia, and every object in the universe has it.

A neighbour's car pulled up with a jerk, and Kofi saw the shopping bag on the back seat slide forward onto the floor. The car had stopped, but the bag, in obedience to inertia, had carried on moving at the old speed until something got in its way. This is exactly why people in cars wear seat belts, which give the body a gentle, steady force instead of a sudden, violent one.

Zainab marked two trees that stood fifty metres apart and told Kofi to cycle past them at a steady pace while she timed him. He covered the distance in ten seconds, which meant that he was travelling at about five metres per second. To convert that into something more familiar, it comes to around eighteen kilometres an hour.

Ama arrived on her skateboard, rolled toward Kofi at exactly the speed at which he was cycling toward her, and the two of them passed with a wave. Their speeds were identical, Zainab said, yet their velocities were opposite, because velocity is speed together with a direction. Physicists need both, since a push to the north has quite different results from a push to the south.

Kofi started from a standstill and pedalled harder and harder, so that the bicycle moved a little faster with every passing second. Zainab shouted from the roadside that this gradual gain in speed was acceleration, which she defined as the rate at which velocity changes. Cars, rockets and falling apples all accelerate, and so does anything that slows down.

At the end of the road Kofi swung round a long bend without speeding up or slowing down at all. Zainab insisted that he was accelerating anyway, because his direction was changing and therefore his velocity was changing as well. It is a strange idea at first, but it explains why you feel pushed sideways when a car takes a sharp corner.

Zainab drew a small table in her notebook showing that Kofi's speed had climbed from nothing to five metres per second in exactly five seconds. Dividing the gain in speed by the time it took gave an acceleration of one metre per second, every second, which she wrote as one metre per second squared. Kofi laughed and said that it sounded much more difficult than it felt on the bike.

Zainab summed up the lesson so far by explaining that a force is simply a push or a pull, and that forces are measured in units called newtons, after Isaac Newton. Whenever the velocity of an object changes, she said, some force must be responsible, and whenever there is no force the velocity stays exactly as it was. The next question, which Kofi was eager to answer, was exactly how much a particular force could change the motion of a particular thing.

Outside Mr Boateng's corner shop, Kofi tried pushing an empty trolley and then one stacked high with tins of tomatoes. The empty trolley leapt forward at the slightest shove, while the loaded one crept away so slowly that he had to lean on it with his whole body. The same push, Zainab observed, had produced very different accelerations, and the difference was the mass.

Next Kofi pushed the same empty trolley twice, first with a polite little nudge and then with every ounce of his strength. The second push set it racing along the pavement, and Zainab pointed out that when the mass stays the same, doubling the force doubles the acceleration. This simple link between pushing and speeding up is at the heart of Newton's second law.

Mr Boateng lent Zainab a pencil, and she wrote on the side of a paper bag that force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. This tidy sentence, which physicists abbreviate to F equals m a, is the whole of Newton's second law, and it works for everything from skateboards to spaceships. Kofi copied it carefully into his notebook, though he did not yet see how powerful it was.

To try out the law, Zainab imagined a box with a mass of ten kilograms and a push of twenty newtons, and she asked Kofi to find the acceleration. He divided the force by the mass, as the rule suggested, and found that the box would speed up by two metres per second, every second. Kofi grinned, for it was the first time that a physics sum had come out the way he expected.

Ama kicked a tennis ball across the grass and then, with the same swing of her leg, kicked a heavy ball of exactly the same size. The first one sailed far across the park, but the second rolled only a few metres, because its greater mass made it far harder to accelerate. Mass, Zainab said, is a measure of how much an object resists any change in its motion.

On the school field two teams of children were locked in a tug of war, heaving at opposite ends of a thick rope while their teacher cheered. Neither side could win, and the knot in the middle did not move at all, because equal forces in opposite directions cancel each other out. What matters in physics, Zainab said, is the net force, which is what remains after all the pushes and pulls have been added together.

Suddenly a few children on the left slipped on the damp grass and their grip weakened, and the rope began to slide toward the stronger side. The forces were no longer balanced, so a net force appeared and the rope accelerated exactly as the second law predicted. Kofi, who had been watching with growing excitement, realised that he could now explain every tug of war he had ever seen.

Ama lent Kofi her skateboard, and he gave a push against the garden wall and went gliding backward across the pavement. The wall had not moved, yet it had clearly pushed him, because Newton's third law says that whenever one object pushes another, the second pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction. The two forces always come together as a pair, acting on two different objects at the very same instant.

Zainab threaded a long string through a drinking straw, stretched it across the garden, and let a blown-up balloon go. The balloon pushed the air backward out of its neck, and the air pushed the balloon forward in return, so that it zipped along the string with an angry hiss. Kofi insisted on doing it three more times to see whether the law ever failed, and it never did.

A rocket is simply a much bigger balloon, which hurls a stream of hot gas backward at tremendous speed so that the gas pushes the rocket forward. Many people suppose that a rocket needs air to push against, but it does not, which is why rockets work perfectly well in the vacuum of space. Isaac Newton published his three laws of motion in 1687, and engineers still rely on them today.

Friction is the force that acts when two surfaces rub against each other, and it always works against the motion. A bicycle brake presses a pad against the wheel so that friction can slow the bike, and the pad warms up as the energy of movement turns into heat. On smooth ice there is very little friction, so a sliding skater goes on for a long time and finds it hard to stop.

It would be a mistake to think of friction as an enemy, because without it we could not walk, drive, or even hold a pencil. Every step Kofi took depended on the rough rubber of his shoes gripping the pavement, which is why a wet floor or a patch of ice can send a person flying. Engineers spend their working lives deciding where to add friction and where to take it away.

On a chilly corner Zainab told Kofi to rub his hands together as fast as he could, and then to press them against his cheeks. The warmth he felt came directly from friction, which turns the energy of movement into heat, and it is the same reason that a drill grows hot and that a meteor glows as it rushes through the air. Our distant ancestors used this very idea to start their fires, by rubbing one wooden stick against another until it smouldered.

An apple dropped from a branch and bounced at Kofi's feet, which reminded Zainab of a famous story about Isaac Newton. He is said to have wondered why an apple always falls straight down toward the ground, and why the same pull might not reach all the way to the Moon. Gravity is the attraction between any two things that have mass, and the enormous Earth pulls on everything near it.

Kofi stood on the low garden wall and let go of a heavy ball and a light ball at the same moment, fully expecting the heavy one to land first. They hit the grass together, just as the Italian scientist Galileo is said to have discovered some four hundred years ago. A heavier object feels a stronger pull from gravity, but it also has more inertia, and the two effects cancel exactly.

A feather drifts down slowly, and this seems to contradict Galileo until we remember that the air pushes against the feather far more than it pushes against a stone. In 1971, on the airless surface of the Moon, an Apollo astronaut dropped a hammer and a falling feather side by side, and the two reached the ground at the same moment. Without any air to get in the way, Zainab said, gravity treats every object alike, whether it is a feather or a hammer.

A falling stone does not drop at a steady speed but goes faster and faster, and near the surface of the Earth its speed grows by about ten metres per second in every second. After one second it is travelling at about ten metres per second, after two at twenty, and after three at thirty, so long as the air does not slow it down. This steady gain is called the acceleration of gravity, and Zainab said it is the same for every falling object.

As a falling object gathers speed, the air pushes back harder and harder, until at last the push of the air balances the pull of gravity. From then on the object falls at a steady speed and no longer accelerates, and a parachute is wide enough that this steady speed is slow enough to survive. Kofi decided that a parachute is simply friction with the air, put to very good use.

High over the hill Kofi spotted the pale Moon in the daytime sky and asked why it never fell down. Zainab explained that it does fall, all the time, but it also moves sideways so fast that the curving Earth keeps slipping away beneath it. Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain firing balls faster and faster until one flew all the way around the world, and that, in essence, is an orbit.

Zainab ended the morning's lesson by making a distinction that most people never learn, which is that mass is the amount of matter in an object, whereas weight is the force with which gravity pulls on it. On the Moon, where gravity is about one sixth as strong, Kofi would weigh about six times less, although he would contain exactly the same amount of matter. His mass, the amount of matter in his body, would not change by a single gram, wherever he travelled.

By midday the cycling had left Kofi hungry, so the two of them settled on a bench in the park and Zainab began the second of her big ideas. Energy, she said, is the ability to cause change, whether that means moving a bicycle, warming a room, or lighting a lamp. It is one of the most useful ideas in the whole of science, and it explains why everything in the universe happens.

Zainab went on to explain that energy turns up in many different disguises, among them movement, heat, light, sound and electricity. It can also be stored quietly, as in a battery, a bar of chocolate, a stretched spring or a rock balanced on a cliff, waiting for the moment when it is needed. Kofi noticed that every one of these examples involved something changing, whether it was a position, a temperature or a speed.

The energy that a moving object possesses because of its motion is called kinetic energy, and it depends on both the mass and the speed. Two cyclists of the same weight may be riding along the same road, but the one who is racing has far more kinetic energy than the one who is dawdling. Kinetic comes from a Greek word for movement, so the name is easy to remember.

When the speed is doubled the kinetic energy becomes four times larger, because the speed appears twice in the calculation, as half the mass times the speed times the speed. A car travelling at sixty kilometres an hour therefore has four times the energy of the same car at thirty, which is why a fast crash does so much more damage than a slow one. This is the reason for speed limits near schools, where a small difference in speed can mean a very large difference in danger.

A lorry rumbled past while Kofi was eating, and Zainab pointed out that it was travelling no faster than a bicycle but carried vastly more energy. Kinetic energy grows in step with mass, so a vehicle that weighs a hundred times more has a hundred times the energy at the same speed. That is why a lorry needs a much greater distance to stop, and why its driver must always leave a wide gap.

Ama, who had been to a fair the previous summer, described the slow climb of a roller coaster car to the very top of the track. At that point it has stored a great deal of potential energy, which is the energy an object holds because of its position, and which is ready to turn into movement the instant it begins to roll down. The thrill of the whole ride is really nothing more than that stored energy being released in a rush.

After lunch they set off up the steepest hill in the town, and Kofi pushed his bicycle with rising breathlessness. Every metre he climbed cost him energy, which did not vanish but was stored in the height he and his bicycle had gained, and the higher or the heavier the load, the more energy was needed. At the top, Zainab said, he would hold more potential energy than he had at the bottom.

Halfway up the hill Zainab stopped to show him that height is not the only place where energy can hide. A rubber band, a spring or a bent bow stores elastic energy when it is stretched or squashed, and releases it the moment it springs back to its normal shape. She pulled a paper pellet back against a rubber band, and with a twang it shot off into the bushes.

Energy is measured in units called joules, named after the English physicist James Joule, and one joule is roughly the energy needed to lift a small apple up through a metre. The climb up the hill had cost Kofi and his bicycle tens of thousands of joules, a figure that made him feel unusually proud of his tired legs. Joule was a brewer's son from near Manchester who spent years measuring heat and energy with extraordinary care.

At last they reached the summit, where the wind blew freshly and the whole town lay spread out like a map beneath them. Kofi's bicycle, which stood leaning against a rock, had gained a great deal of potential energy during the climb, and that energy was now ready to be released. Zainab grinned and told him that the road down would show him exactly where it all went.

Kofi pointed the bicycle down the hill, took his feet off the pedals, and let the road do the work. With every metre he descended the potential energy that he had earned on the way up was converted into kinetic energy, and the wind rushed louder past his ears. By the bottom he was moving so fast that he squeezed the brakes with real respect.

Back at the park Zainab hung a smooth stone from a low branch by a length of string and set it swinging gently to and fro. At the highest point of each swing the stone paused for an instant, full of stored energy, and at the lowest point it raced along at top speed, full of kinetic energy. The two kinds of energy took turns again and again, like two children sharing a single seat on a seesaw.

Zainab now announced the most important rule in the whole of physics, which is called the conservation of energy. Energy is never created and never destroyed, she said, but only changed from one form to another, so that the total amount in a closed system always stays the same. Scientists have tested this law for more than a century and a half, and it has never once failed.

Kofi noticed that the swings of the stone were getting smaller, and he asked whether that broke the great law. Zainab told him that the missing energy had not disappeared at all, because the stone had pushed the air aside and rubbed against the branch, and these tiny frictions had warmed both by an amount too small to feel. In a great many cases, then, energy that seems to have been lost has really become heat that is spread through the surroundings.

Ama pointed out that every roller coaster has its tallest hill at the start, and Zainab agreed that this was no accident. Each time the car rolls along the track, friction and air resistance turn a little of its energy into heat, so it can never climb quite as high as it began. Designers have to build the later hills lower, or the car would stall halfway up.

Kofi dropped a rubber ball onto the stone path and counted nine bounces, each one a little lower than the last, before the ball finally rolled to a halt. At every impact a small part of its energy escaped as sound and as a faint warming of the ball and the ground, leaving less for the next rebound. No energy vanished, but it was spread out in forms that could not bounce the ball again.

For hundreds of years inventors have tried to build a perpetual motion machine, a device that would run for ever without fuel and even produce a surplus of energy. Every design has failed, and Zainab explained that the failure is no accident but a consequence of the conservation of energy, which forbids the creation of energy from nothing. Anyone who offers you such a machine, she added with a smile, is either mistaken or selling something.

Kofi's bicycle carried a small lamp that glowed whenever the back wheel was turning, and Zainab used it to show how energy travels along a chain of changes. The energy in his breakfast went into his legs, from his legs into the spinning wheel, and from the wheel into the light and a trace of warmth. At every link in the chain a little of the energy escaped as heat, but the total amount never changed.

Ama set a row of marbles in a groove, touching one another, and rolled a single marble into one end of the line. The marbles in the middle barely twitched, yet the marble at the far end shot off, because the energy of the first had been handed from marble to marble in a few thousandths of a second. Kofi stared, for it looked like magic and was in fact simply the conservation of energy at work.

Zainab compared energy to money in the bank, where the amount can be shifted from one account to another and exchanged for different currencies without ever being created or destroyed. About a hundred years ago the German mathematician Emmy Noether showed that this law is linked to the fact that the rules of physics do not change from one moment to the next. Kofi wrote the comparison in his notebook, drew a small picture of a piggy bank beside it, and underlined it twice.

Back at the bench Kofi unwrapped a second sandwich and ate it with great satisfaction. Food stores chemical energy in the bonds between its molecules, and the body releases that energy slowly, using it to move the muscles, to power the brain and to keep the whole body at a steady, comfortable warmth. Without a regular supply of food, as every hungry boy knows, nothing in the body works properly for very long.

A single sandwich, Zainab told him, holds well over a million joules of chemical energy, which sounds like an enormous treasure. Yet a human body spends such a sum surprisingly quickly, because every heartbeat, every breath and every step uses a little of it, and the rest becomes the warmth that keeps us alive. The sandwich in his hand, in other words, was a small tank of fuel.

Zainab astonished Kofi by saying that a person sitting quietly gives off heat at about the same rate as a bright old-fashioned light bulb, roughly one hundred watts. That is why a crowded room soon grows warm, even when nobody is running or shouting, and why a cold night is so much better spent in company. Kofi looked down at his hands, half expecting them to begin glowing like the filament of a very small bulb.

Power measures how quickly energy is used or changed, and it is counted in watts, where one watt means one joule every second. A modern light bulb may need only about ten watts, whereas an electric kettle may use two or three thousand, which is why it can boil water in minutes. A cheap appliance that runs for a long time can therefore cost more than an expensive one that is only used briefly.

Zainab drew a simple rule in the dust beside the bench: energy used equals power multiplied by time. A kettle with a high power rating runs for only a few minutes, so a small lamp left burning all night can quietly use up as much energy as several kettles. Electricity companies measure this in kilowatt-hours, which means a thousand watts used steadily for one hour.

Coal, oil and natural gas are known as fossil fuels, and they were formed over millions of years from the buried remains of ancient plants and tiny sea creatures. The energy locked inside them originally came from sunshine that was captured by those living things, which means that every time we burn petrol we release sunlight from the distant past. The supply is limited, and burning it also adds carbon dioxide to the air.

Green plants are tiny solar factories, for their leaves catch sunlight and use its energy to build sugars out of carbon dioxide and water, in a process called photosynthesis. Animals eat the plants, and people eat both, so that nearly all of the energy in nearly every meal began as light that left the Sun about eight minutes before it arrived. Kofi looked at the half-eaten sandwich in his hand with a new respect for the tiny factories that had made it.

From the bench they could see a row of wind turbines turning slowly on a ridge and a field of solar panels glittering in the afternoon sun. Both depend on the Sun, which heats the air unevenly and so creates the winds, and which also lifts water from the oceans to fall as rain on the hills and fill the rivers that drive hydroelectric dams. Almost every source of energy we use, apart from a few exceptions, is sunshine in some disguise.

There are a few exceptions to the rule, Zainab admitted, and the tides are one of them, because they are raised mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon. Geothermal energy is another, for it comes from the heat inside the Earth, and nuclear power, which she promised to explain that night, is a third. Kofi added a small note to the envelope, marked with a question about the nuclear one.

No machine turns all of its energy into what we want, and the share that does the useful job is called its efficiency. An old filament bulb wasted most of its energy as heat, whereas a modern LED gives the same light for a fraction of the electricity, so a household can save a great deal simply by changing its bulbs. Using energy wisely, said Zainab, is not a sacrifice but a kind of cleverness.

In the late afternoon they cycled back to Zainab's kitchen, where she filled the kettle and switched it on, and the third idea arrived with the first puff of steam. Everything is made of molecules, she said, and these tiny particles are never still, so what we call heat is really the jostling and jiggling of countless molecules too small to see. The hotter something is, the more energetically its molecules move, and the more violently they push against everything near them.

Zainab placed two glasses on the table, one filled with hot water and one with cold, and let a single drop of ink fall into each. In the hot glass the colour unfurled and spread within moments, whereas in the cold glass it drifted outward lazily, because the water molecules there were jostling the ink around much more slowly. Kofi could not see a single molecule, yet he could see what they were doing.

Temperature, Zainab explained, tells us how fast the molecules are moving on average, whereas heat is the total energy of that movement and the energy that flows from one thing to another. A cup of boiling tea is hotter than a bath of lukewarm water, yet the bath holds far more heat, because it contains millions of millions of times as many molecules. Mixing up the two ideas, she said, is one of the commonest mistakes in science.

The Celsius scale, which was named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius, divides the range between the freezing and boiling of water into one hundred equal steps. Water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred when the air pressure is that of sea level, and a healthy human body holds steady at about thirty-seven. Some countries still use the Fahrenheit scale, which puts the same two points at thirty-two and two hundred and twelve.

Zainab worked out that it takes about four thousand joules to warm a kilogram of water by one degree, so heating a litre from room temperature to boiling needs roughly three hundred and fifty thousand joules. A kettle rated at two thousand watts supplies two thousand joules every second, so the job takes close to three minutes, just as Kofi had always found. It was the first time he had ever checked a sum against a kettle.

Zainab reminded Kofi of last summer's beach, where the sand had scorched his feet while the sea beside it felt delightfully cool, although both had been in the same sunshine all day. Water has an unusually large capacity for storing heat, which means it needs far more energy than sand to rise by a single degree. This is also why coastal towns tend to have milder winters and cooler summers than places inland.

Ice, liquid water and steam look entirely different, yet each consists of the very same molecules, arranged in three different ways. In ice the molecules are locked in a rigid pattern and only tremble, in water they slip and slide past one another, and in steam they fly about freely in all directions. These three forms are called the states of matter, and almost any substance can pass through all of them.

Kofi dropped ice cubes into his lemonade and noticed that the drink grew cold at once. Melting ice absorbs a large quantity of heat without changing its own temperature, which stays at zero degrees until the last crystal has gone, and that absorbed heat is taken from the lemonade. Physicists call it latent heat, a name that suggests the energy is hiding in the change itself.

High on a mountain the air above us is thinner and presses down less firmly, so water begins to boil at a temperature well below one hundred degrees. At around three thousand metres it bubbles at about ninety, which is why climbers complain that their tea is never properly hot and their rice takes ages to cook. A pressure cooker does the opposite, raising the pressure so that the water gets hotter before it boils.

When a liquid evaporates, it is the fastest and most energetic molecules that escape from the surface, so the molecules left behind have less energy and the liquid grows cooler. That is how sweat cools the body on a hot day, and why Kofi's wet hair felt chilly when the breeze blew, and why blowing across a hot drink helps it to cool. Even in something as ordinary as a wet head of hair and a hot drink, Zainab remarked, the idea of moving molecules explained everything.

Kofi left a metal spoon standing in his mug of hot tea and, a minute later, found that the handle had become warm to the touch. Heat always travels from a hotter object to a colder one, and it never flows the other way unless something forces it, which is why a cup of tea cools down but never heats itself up. This one-way traffic of energy is the key to the whole of the third idea, and Kofi would meet it again and again.

Kofi laid one hand on the metal leg of the table and the other on a wooden chair, and the metal felt distinctly colder, although a thermometer showed that both were at the temperature of the room. Metal is a good conductor, so it draws heat out of your fingers very quickly, whereas wood conducts so slowly that your skin barely loses any. What we feel is not temperature but the speed at which heat leaves us.

In conduction, the molecules at the hot end of a solid vibrate more vigorously and jostle their neighbours, which then jostle theirs, so that the energy is passed along like a message in a crowd. Metals are particularly good at this, because they also contain free electrons that carry energy quickly through the material. That is why the handle of a metal saucepan can burn your fingers, and why cooks prefer handles made of wood or plastic.

A jumper does not produce any warmth of its own, but it traps a great deal of still air among its fibres, and since air is a poor conductor the heat of your body leaks out slowly. Double-glazed windows and the fluffy material in a loft use the same trick, and a vacuum flask goes one step further by removing the air from between its walls. Insulation, in other words, is simply the art of making heat flow so slowly that it is hardly noticed.

When air is heated its molecules move apart, so it becomes less dense than the cooler air around it and floats upward, rather as a cork floats in water. A hot air balloon exploits this directly, while the same rising and sinking, called convection, circulates heat in a heated room and in a pan of water on the stove. Convection can only work in a fluid, which means in either a liquid or a gas, because solids cannot flow.

Zainab sketched a room with a radiator beneath the window, and showed how the air next to it warms, rises to the ceiling, drifts across the room, cools, and sinks again to the floor. This continuous loop of moving air is called a convection current, and it distributes the heat far more effectively than conduction could. It also explains why the ceiling of a room is always warmer than the floor.

The third way in which heat travels is radiation, in which warm objects give off invisible rays of infrared that carry energy through space without needing any material to pass it along. Sunshine reaches us only by radiation, across about one hundred and fifty million kilometres of nearly empty space, and a fire warms your face in the same fashion. Even Kofi, sitting quietly in the kitchen with his notebook, was radiating a steady stream of heat in every direction.

On the washing line two shirts hung side by side in the sunshine, one black and one white, and when Kofi touched them the black one was noticeably warmer. Dark surfaces absorb most of the radiation that falls on them, whereas pale and shiny surfaces reflect much of it, which is why people in hot countries often wear white and why a space blanket looks like silver foil. Colour, it seems, is also a question of heat, and the choice of a shirt can make a real difference on a sunny day.

Left alone on the kitchen table, Kofi's tea gradually cooled until a thermometer dipped into it showed exactly the same reading as the one hanging on the wall. Heat flows only while there is a difference in temperature, and once the difference has gone the flow stops, a condition that physicists call thermal equilibrium. It is the natural resting place of every warm object and every cold one.

If heat is the movement of molecules, there must be a limit to how cold anything can get, which is when the molecules have given up as much movement as they possibly can. This temperature, called absolute zero, is about minus 273 degrees Celsius, and the Kelvin scale, named after Lord Kelvin, starts counting from it. The coldest natural temperature ever recorded on the Earth is about minus 89 degrees, in Antarctica, which is warm compared with absolute zero.

Kofi poured a little milk into Zainab's coffee and watched the white swirls spread and fade until the whole cup had turned a uniform pale brown. No amount of stirring, in either direction, would ever persuade the milk to gather itself back into a separate cloud. Zainab said that this one-way street is the most puzzling and most important feature of the whole subject of heat.

A tidy bedroom turns into a messy one without any effort at all, whereas the opposite never happens unless somebody works hard. The reason is a matter of numbers, since there are only a few ways to arrange the books neatly on the shelf and millions of ways to scatter them across the floor. Disorder wins not because of any law of laziness, but because it is overwhelmingly more probable.

If you shuffle a pack of cards, the chance of finishing with every card in perfect order is so tiny that it will almost certainly never happen in your lifetime. Physicists use the word entropy for the amount of disorder in a system, a term coined by the German scientist Rudolf Clausius in 1865, and the second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a closed system tends to increase. It is not a law that forbids the impossible, but a law of probability applied on a truly gigantic scale.

When a hot cup of tea cools, its energy does not disappear but spreads out among the countless molecules of the air in the room, where it raises the temperature by a tiny and unnoticeable amount. Spread-out energy is far less useful than concentrated energy, for the warm room could never boil a kettle, although the tea once could. In this sense, every ordinary event, from a cooling cup to a falling leaf, makes the world a little more disordered.

A car engine burns fuel to make a very hot gas, and it uses the flow of heat from the hot gas to the cooler surroundings to push the wheels round. The second law makes it impossible to turn all of the heat into movement, for some must always be thrown away into a colder place, which is why exhaust pipes and radiators are so hot. Every engine, whatever its design, needs somewhere cooler into which it can dump its waste heat.

In a typical petrol car only about a quarter to a third of the fuel's energy actually turns the wheels, while the rest escapes as hot exhaust gases and as warmth from the engine and the radiator. This is a limit imposed by the second law and not merely a failing of engineers, although they work hard to get as close to it as possible. Electric motors are much more efficient, because they do not have to turn heat into movement.

A refrigerator seems to break the rule that heat flows from hot to cold, because it takes heat from the cool inside and delivers it to the warmer kitchen. It can do this only because it is driven by electricity, and the energy it uses is released along with the extracted heat through the warm grille at the back. Overall, therefore, a fridge makes the kitchen a little warmer, and entropy still increases.

Zainab asked Kofi to imagine a film of a cup falling from a table and smashing on the stone floor, and then the same film played in reverse. The backward version looks absurd, because the pieces would leap together and fly back onto the table, and our sense that time has a direction is closely connected to the growth of entropy. The laws of motion work either way, but the story of heat does not.

Kofi pointed out that living creatures are astonishingly well organised, which seems to contradict the law that disorder always grows. The answer is that a living thing is not a closed system, because it takes in energy and gives out heat, so its order is paid for by more disorder outside. A living body is like a tidy desk kept tidy only by constant effort.

Zainab crossed the third line off the envelope and gathered the idea into one sentence, saying that heat always flows from hot to cold and that the universe drifts steadily toward greater disorder. Kofi's tea had long since gone cold and the afternoon sun was sinking toward the roofs, so they set out along the lane toward the river, with Ama and her dog Biscuit running ahead. The fourth idea, waves, was waiting there to greet them, quite literally, in the rippling surface of the water.

At the pond, Kofi dropped a stone and watched the ripples run out in circles, and Zainab used them to introduce the fourth big idea, the wave. A wave is a disturbance that moves from place to place and carries energy with it, but it does not carry the material along. A floating leaf bobs up and down as the ripples pass underneath, and then stays more or less where it was.

Ama borrowed a long rope from the boathouse and gave one end to Kofi, then flicked her own end sharply upward. A bump raced along the rope toward him and shook his hand as it arrived, although no part of the rope itself had travelled from one end to the other. Each piece had simply moved up and down and passed the movement to its neighbour.

Ama then stretched a coiled spring toy across the grass and pushed one end sharply forward, and a squeezed patch of coils travelled along its length. In this kind of wave, which is called longitudinal, the material moves back and forth in the same direction as the wave, whereas the rope and the pond ripples are examples of the sideways kind, known as transverse waves. Sound, as Kofi would soon discover for himself, belongs in the first group, the longitudinal kind.

With a stick Zainab drew a wavy line in the damp sand at the water's edge and named its parts for Kofi. The highest points are the crests and the lowest points the troughs, the distance from one crest to the next is the wavelength, and the height of a crest above the middle line is the amplitude. The bigger the amplitude, she said, the more energy the wave carries, which is why big waves can knock a swimmer over.

The number of waves that pass a fixed point every second is the frequency, and it is measured in hertz, in honour of the German physicist Heinrich Hertz. Zainab and Kofi counted two ripples a second passing a twig, and since the crests were ten centimetres apart, the ripples were travelling at twenty centimetres per second. Speed, she explained, is simply the frequency multiplied by the wavelength, and this rule holds for every kind of wave.

The waves on the pond move at a gentle walking pace, but a tsunami caused by an undersea earthquake can cross the open ocean at roughly eight hundred kilometres an hour. In deep water it may be only a low swell that a ship hardly notices, but as it reaches the shallows it slows down and piles up into a towering wall of water. Waves are not always the gentle, harmless thing that a pond makes them seem.

Kofi dropped two pebbles into the pond a short distance apart, and the two circles of ripples spread out until they overlapped. Where two crests met, the water rose higher, and where a crest met a trough they cancelled and the surface stayed almost flat, a behaviour called interference. Afterward each set of ripples continued onward as if nothing had happened, which is something that solid objects can never do.

When the ripples reached the stone wall at the edge of the pond, they did not stop but turned back toward the centre, leaving at the same angle at which they had arrived. This bouncing of a wave from a barrier is called reflection, and it is the reason why you see your face in a mirror and why a shout can come back from a distant hill. Waves of every kind, from sound to light, do exactly the same thing when they meet a barrier.

Ama piled stones into two low walls with a narrow gap between them and sent ripples toward the opening, and on the far side the waves spread out into neat half circles. A wave that passes through a gap about as wide as its own wavelength bends outward in this way, an effect named diffraction, which explains why you can hear someone talking around a corner. Sound waves are long enough to bend easily around corners, whereas the much shorter waves of light hardly bend at all.

An earthquake sends waves rippling through the solid body of the Earth, and sensitive instruments called seismographs record them on the far side of the planet. By studying how fast the waves travel and where they bend or fail to arrive, scientists have discovered that the Earth has a liquid outer core and a solid inner one, though no human could ever dig that deep. Waves of many kinds, it seems, can carry news from places that no human being could ever visit.

Far across the valley a storm was gathering over the hills, and Kofi saw a thin white flash of lightning split the dark clouds. He counted slowly to nine before the thunder rolled over the water, because light arrives almost instantly, whereas sound crawls through the air at a mere third of a kilometre every second. Nine seconds, therefore, meant that the storm was still about three kilometres away, and Zainab said that they had time to enjoy the show.

Zainab told Kofi to hum a low note with his fingertips resting on his throat, and he felt a distinct buzzing under the skin. Every sound begins with something vibrating, whether it is a voice box, a drum skin or a guitar string, and the vibrating object pushes and pulls the neighbouring air, which passes the disturbance on in a longitudinal wave. The sound that reaches an ear is a pattern of tiny changes in air pressure.

Zainab described an old experiment in which an electric bell is rung inside a glass jar while a pump slowly removes the air, and the sound grows fainter and fainter until the bell can be seen ringing in silence. Sound needs a material to carry it, whether air, water or a solid, and since space is almost a perfect vacuum, it is silent out there. The roaring explosions in space films, she added with a smile, are therefore quite unrealistic, since nothing could carry the sound.

Ama walked to the far end of the long iron railing beside the river and tapped it with a stone while Kofi pressed his ear against the metal. He heard two taps, a sharp one almost at once and a fainter one a fraction of a second later, because sound travels through steel about fifteen times faster than through air. In water, Zainab added, it travels about four times as fast as in air.

Ama had brought her guitar, and Zainab used it to show that the pitch of a note, meaning how high or low it sounds, depends on the frequency of the vibration. A short, tight string vibrates many times a second and sings a high note, a long loose one vibrates slowly and gives a deep one, and plucking harder makes a larger wave, which we hear as a louder sound. Pitch and loudness are therefore quite separate things, controlled by the frequency and the size of the wave.

Human ears can detect vibrations from about twenty to twenty thousand hertz, and anything higher, called ultrasound, passes unheard. When Zainab blew a silent dog whistle, Biscuit instantly pricked up his ears, although Kofi heard nothing at all, and the bats that began to flit over the river at dusk use sounds that are higher still. The world is full of sounds that people never notice, simply because our ears were not built to hear them.

Kofi cupped his hands around his mouth, shouted toward the old stone bridge, and heard his own voice come back after about half a second. Sound travels roughly 170 metres in that time, but the echo had made a round trip, so Zainab calculated that the bridge must be about eighty-five metres away. An echo is simply reflected sound, and the delay tells us the distance of the surface that sent it back.

Bats navigate in the dark by sending out high squeaks and listening carefully for the echoes, which tell them where the trees, walls and insects are. Humans have copied the trick in sonar, which allows a ship to measure the depth of the sea, and in medical ultrasound, which uses very high sound to make a picture of a baby growing inside its mother. In this way, echoes have been turned into a kind of seeing that works in darkness and in deep water.

On the riverside playground Kofi gave Ama's swing a small push every time it returned to him, and before long she was swinging high above his head. Every object has a natural rhythm at which it likes to move, and when small pushes arrive exactly in time with that rhythm they add up into a very large motion, a phenomenon known as resonance. A singer who sings the right note can even make a wine glass vibrate until it shatters.

Loudness is measured in decibels, and the scale is arranged so that every ten decibels means a tenfold increase in the intensity of the sound. A whisper measures about thirty, ordinary conversation about sixty, and a rock concert more than a hundred, and long exposure to sounds above roughly eighty-five decibels can damage the delicate hairs in the inner ear. Zainab urged Kofi to wear ear protection at concerts, because those cells never grow back.

As the sun sank toward the hills, a beam of golden light slanted through the mist along the riverbank, and Zainab used it to introduce her second kind of wave. Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second, which is faster than anything else we know, so sunshine that left the Sun about eight minutes ago has only just arrived. Light from the Moon, which is far closer, needs only a little over a second to reach us.

When the wind died away, the surface of the pond became as smooth as glass, and the trees on the far bank appeared upside down in the water below them. Light travels in straight lines, and a smooth surface reflects each ray so that it leaves at the same angle at which it arrived, keeping the picture sharp, whereas a rough surface scatters the rays. Mirrors do the same thing, with a thin layer of shiny metal behind the glass.

Zainab stood a pencil in a glass of water from her bag, and Kofi saw that it seemed to be broken at the point where it entered the water. Light travels more slowly in water than in air, so the rays change direction as they cross the surface, a bending that is called refraction. It is also why a swimming pool always looks shallower than it really is.

Sunlight appears white, but it is really a mixture of every colour, and each colour is a wave of a slightly different length, with red waves the longest and violet the shortest. Raindrops act like tiny prisms, bending each colour by a different amount and spreading the light into a rainbow that arcs across the sky. If you ever see one, remember that your position decides which drops send the colours to you.

The gases in the air scatter short blue waves of sunlight much more strongly than long red ones, which spreads blue light across the whole sky and makes the day look blue. At sunset the light must pass through a far thicker slice of the atmosphere before it reaches us, so most of the blue is scattered away and the sky glows with the reds and oranges that remain. The colours above Kofi's head, in short, were a free lesson in the physics of waves and the scattering of light.

Zainab drew a long ladder in her notebook to show that visible light is only a very narrow slice of a much larger family of waves. Radio waves, microwaves and infrared have longer wavelengths than light, while ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have shorter ones, yet all of them travel at the same speed through empty space and differ only in wavelength. Our eyes see a tiny window of this spectrum and are blind to the rest.

Infrared radiation, which lies just beyond red light, carries the warmth we feel from a fire and is used in television remote controls and night-vision cameras. Ultraviolet radiation, just beyond violet, has enough energy to damage skin cells, which is why long hours in strong sunshine cause sunburn and why doctors recommend sunscreen, a hat and some shade. Kofi pointed his phone camera at a remote control and saw a faint purple glow.

Zainab held up the magnifying glass from her bag and showed Kofi how its curved glass bent the parallel rays of sunlight to a bright point on his notebook. A lens makes use of refraction in this way, and it is the principle behind spectacles, cameras, telescopes and microscopes, as well as the living lens inside every human eye. A well-shaped lens can make a distant mountain or a tiny insect seem close at hand.

Inside the eye, a flexible lens focuses incoming light into a small upside-down image on the retina, which is a layer of light-sensitive cells at the back, and the brain turns the signals into the picture we see. Our eyes respond only to the narrow band of colours from red to violet, whereas bees can also see ultraviolet, and many flowers have patterns on their petals that only bees can see. Kofi wondered what else he was missing, hidden in all the colours and rays that his eyes could not detect.

The sun went down in a last blaze of orange, and a single bright star appeared above the river, which meant that the fourth idea was finished. Zainab told Kofi that light is a most surprising kind of wave, because it needs no material to travel through and turns out to be made of electricity and magnetism working together. That, she said, was the fifth idea, and a thunderstorm was already coming to help them with it.

On the way home through the dusk, Zainab took the balloon from her rucksack and told Kofi to rub it hard against his hair, and he laughed as the strands rose up to meet it. This was the first small step into her fifth big idea, electricity and magnetism, which together make up one of the most powerful forces in the world. Rubbing, she said, had moved something invisible and very small from his hair to the balloon, and she promised to show him what it was.

Matter contains two kinds of electric charge, which are named positive and negative, and most objects hold equal amounts of each, so that the effects cancel out. Rubbing two materials together can drag some of the negative charge from one to the other, leaving one slightly positive and the other slightly negative, which is what had happened to Kofi's hair and the balloon. It was Benjamin Franklin who chose these two names, in the eighteenth century, and they have been used ever since.

Zainab rubbed two balloons on her sleeve and hung them side by side on strings, where they swung apart as if each one were afraid of the other. Charges of the same kind repel one another, whereas charges of opposite kinds attract, and this is why a charged balloon sticks to a wall by pulling on the opposite charge it draws out of the surface. The force between charges is far stronger than the pull of gravity between small objects.

Anyone who has shuffled across a nylon carpet in socks and then reached for a metal door handle knows the little crackle and sting of static electricity. The charge collected from the carpet builds up on the body until it finds a path to escape, and it leaps across the gap in a tiny spark that is harmless but surprising. In a completely dark room, Zainab told him, you could even see the tiny flash as the spark leaps across.

The negative charge that moves when objects are rubbed together is carried by electrons, which are extremely light particles found in every atom. The positive charge is carried by protons, which are far heavier and are locked into the atom's centre, so it is nearly always the electrons that move from one object to another. Charge, like energy, is never created or destroyed, but only moved from place to place.

Zainab explained that some materials, called conductors, allow electric charge to move through them freely, and that all of the metals belong to this group, with copper among the best. Others, such as rubber, glass and plastic, are insulators and hold their charge in place, which is why electrical wires are made of copper but are wrapped in plastic. A balloon can be charged by rubbing only because rubber does not let the charge escape.

Inside a thundercloud, strong winds carry tiny crystals of ice and drops of water up and down, and scientists believe that their countless collisions strip away electrons and sort the charge into separate regions. The top of the cloud becomes mostly positive and the bottom mostly negative, creating a colossal electrical pressure, although the details are still studied by researchers. A storm is, in effect, a gigantic balloon rubbing on a gigantic head of hair.

When the electrical pressure grows too great, the air suddenly gives way and a gigantic spark of lightning leaps between the cloud and the ground. The bolt heats the air around its path to roughly thirty thousand degrees Celsius, several times hotter than the surface of the Sun, and this sudden expansion produces the shock wave that we hear as thunder. Kofi counted the seconds in his head as the first low rumble reached them from across the dark valley.

In the middle of the eighteenth century the American writer and scientist Benjamin Franklin proposed that a pointed metal rod fixed to a roof could lead lightning safely down a thick wire to the ground. The idea worked, and lightning rods now protect tall buildings, churches and towers all over the world, which would otherwise be set alight or shattered by direct strikes. Franklin is also said to have flown a kite in a storm, though the story is often exaggerated.

The thunder came closer and the first fat raindrops began to spatter on the path, so the three friends ran for the house. Zainab shouted as they went that the safest places in a lightning storm are inside a solid building or a closed car, and that a tall tree or an open field is the most dangerous. Safe indoors, they stood by the window and watched the sky flash, and the fifth idea was only just beginning.

A tremendous crack of thunder shook the house, the lights flickered, and the whole street was plunged into darkness. Zainab felt her way to a kitchen drawer and found a torch, and its small beam steadied Kofi at once, for it required no wires from the outside world. The torch carried its own supply of electricity in a cylinder of metal, and it was the perfect starting point for the next lesson.

An electric current is a flow of electric charge, which in a wire means a stream of tiny electrons that are pushed along by a battery. They only move if there is a complete loop for them to follow, called a circuit, and a switch works by breaking the loop. When Kofi closed the switch, the lamp lit almost at once, because every electron in the wire began to move together.

Kofi unscrewed the torch and laid its parts out on the kitchen table in the glow of a candle, where they proved to be remarkably few. There were two batteries, a metal spring, a small switch and a bulb, and together these formed one unbroken loop that the charge could follow from one end of a battery back to the other. Press the switch, and the loop closes and the bulb shines; release it, and the loop breaks and the light goes out.

To make the ideas clearer, Zainab compared a circuit to a water pipe, with a pump at one end and a narrow section in the middle. Voltage is the pressure that pushes the charge, current is the amount that flows past a point each second, and resistance is the narrowness that holds the flow back. Raise the pressure and the flow increases, but make the pipe narrower and the flow shrinks.

Voltage is measured in volts, in honour of the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta, and a typical torch battery supplies about one and a half of them. The electricity in the wall sockets of a house is about a hundred and twenty volts in some countries and about two hundred and thirty in others, which is easily enough to cause serious injury. Zainab made Kofi promise solemnly never to poke anything into a socket, and never to touch a switch with wet hands.

The flow of current is measured in amperes, usually shortened to amps, after the French scientist André-Marie Ampère. Multiplying volts by amps gives the power, so a two-thousand-watt kettle on a mains of about two hundred and thirty volts draws nearly nine amps, whereas the torch bulb needs only a fraction of one. Kofi noted down the rule that watts equal volts times amps, and decided that it was the neatest sum he knew.

Zainab showed him that a thin wire resists the flow of current more than a thick one, and that a long wire resists it more than a short one. The unit of resistance is the ohm, named after the German physicist Georg Ohm, whose law says that voltage equals current times resistance, so three volts across six ohms gives half an amp. Kofi found that the simplest sum in the whole subject was also by far the most useful one.

When Kofi connected two bulbs one after the other in a single loop, they glowed rather dimly, because the battery's push was shared between them, and if one was removed the other went out. When he arranged them on separate branches, each shone brightly, and unscrewing one left the other undisturbed, which is how the lights in a house are connected so that one failure does not plunge every room into darkness. These two ways of wiring a circuit are called series and parallel, and engineers choose between them every day.

Inside every battery two different materials are separated by a chemical, and a reaction between them pushes electrons through the outside circuit, converting stored chemical energy into electrical energy. The first real battery was built by Volta in about the year 1800, from a pile of metal discs, and when the reaction runs out the battery is flat. A rechargeable battery reverses the reaction when it is plugged in, which makes it more useful over many years.

When the lights flickered back on, Kofi dropped bread into the toaster and watched its thin wires glow orange, which was the electrical resistance turning electrical energy into heat. The same effect is used deliberately in a plug fuse, which contains a thin wire designed to melt when the current becomes dangerously large, cutting the circuit before the cables overheat. Zainab told him that it is a small piece of metal that is willing to sacrifice itself.

Zainab produced the magnet from her rucksack and let Kofi play with it beside a second one, and the two seemed to have minds of their own. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract, exactly as with positive and negative charges, though the two forces are not the same. Cut a magnet in half, and each half grows two poles of its own.

On a sheet of paper laid across the magnet Zainab sprinkled a pinch of fine iron filings, and they arranged themselves in beautiful curved lines running from one pole to the other. The pattern reveals the magnetic field, a region of space in which the magnet exerts its force, and this force acts strongly on iron, nickel and cobalt but not on copper, wood or most other materials. A field, in other words, is the invisible reach of a force, spreading out through the space around its source.

Zainab gave Kofi a small compass from her pocket and watched the needle swing and settle toward the north. The Earth itself behaves like an enormous magnet, probably because of the slow movement of molten iron in its core, and the needle simply lines up with the field that this produces. Sailors have trusted such needles for many centuries, long before anyone understood why they worked.

Zainab laid the compass beside a wire and then connected the wire to a battery, and at once the needle swung away from north. In 1820 the Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted noticed exactly this during a lecture, and it was the first proof that electricity and magnetism are connected, for a current produces a magnetic field in the space around it. Kofi felt the hair stand up on the back of his neck when he realised how important that small swing had been.

Zainab wound about forty turns of wire around a long iron nail and joined the two ends to a battery, whereupon the nail began to lift paper pins from the table. A coil of wire carrying current produces a magnetic field, and the iron core concentrates it, so the result is an electromagnet, which is far stronger than the single wire alone. When the current is switched off, the magnetism vanishes and all of the pins drop back onto the table at once.

The great advantage of an electromagnet is that it can be turned on and off, and made stronger or weaker, simply by changing the current. A scrapyard crane uses an enormous one to lift a whole car and drop it where it is needed, while smaller ones are found in doorbells, loudspeakers and the powerful scanners that doctors use to look inside the body. Some of the fastest trains in the world even float a few centimetres above their tracks, held up by electromagnets.

A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a sideways push, and an electric motor is simply a clever arrangement of coils and magnets that uses this push to keep a shaft spinning round. Motors turn the fan in a computer, the drum of a washing machine and the wheels of an electric car, and they are far more efficient than engines that burn fuel. Zainab pointed out that nearly every home contains dozens of them, hidden inside toys, clocks, tools and kitchen machines.

Zainab connected a coil of wire to a tiny lamp and moved a magnet rapidly in and out of it, and the lamp flickered into life even though no battery was involved. In 1831 the English scientist Michael Faraday discovered that a changing magnetic field makes a current flow in a wire, an effect called electromagnetic induction, and it is the secret behind the generation of almost all our electricity. It is, in a sense, the exact reverse of the motor, since movement is now being turned into electricity.

A power station is essentially a giant version of Zainab's experiment, in which a huge magnet is spun inside great coils of wire by a turbine driven by steam, water or wind. Almost everything that produces electricity, from a coal furnace to a hydroelectric dam, is just a way of turning a magnet, and the dynamo on a bicycle uses the same principle on a tiny scale. Kofi, it turned out, had been pedalling a small generator all day long without even knowing it.

In the nineteenth century it was discovered that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field makes an electric field, so the two can sustain each other as they move through space. The result is an electromagnetic wave, and light, radio signals and the waves that carry your phone calls are all examples of it. So the force that holds the balloon to Kofi's hair is the same one that makes sunshine.

The storm rumbled away over the hills, the clouds tore open, and Kofi and Zainab stepped into the dripping garden under a sky already scattered with stars. Zainab picked a single bead of rain from a leaf and announced the sixth and last idea, which is that everything in the universe, from the grass to the stars, is made of atoms. They are so small that no ordinary microscope, however powerful it may be, can show a single one of them.

The Greek thinker Democritus suggested atoms more than two thousand years ago, but he had no proof, and for centuries many scientists doubted them. In the 1820s the botanist Robert Brown noticed specks of pollen jiggling in water, and in 1905 Albert Einstein showed that the dance was caused by the unseen bombardment of water molecules, which turned the doubters into believers. The jiggle, which is known as Brownian motion, can still be seen today with any decent microscope and a little patience.

A typical human hair is about eighty thousandths of a millimetre across, which works out to roughly half a million atoms laid side by side. The numbers become even stranger in a drop of rain, which holds around a thousand billion billion atoms, a quantity so vast that it dwarfs the number of grains of sand on every beach in the world. It is hard to picture, and Zainab admitted that physicists find it hard too.

Zainab asked Kofi to imagine an atom blown up to the size of a great stadium, with a tiny nucleus at its centre and a haze of electrons around it. The nucleus would be no bigger than a grain of sand in the middle of the pitch, and the rest of the stadium would be empty, which means that every solid thing is mostly empty space. Solid objects only feel solid because of the strong electric forces between the electrons of their atoms.

The nucleus is built from two kinds of particle, positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, which are held together by a very powerful force that acts only over short distances. Orbiting outside is a cloud of negatively charged electrons, which are about two thousand times lighter than a proton, and in a normal atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so that the charges cancel. Kofi drew the picture three times in his notebook, labelling the nucleus and the electrons, so that he would remember it.

There are about one hundred and eighteen known kinds of atom, called the elements, and they are arranged in the famous periodic table, a system devised by the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. What decides the element is the number of protons in the nucleus, so that an atom with one proton is hydrogen, with six it is carbon, and with eight it is oxygen. Everything that we know, from oceans to orchestras, is built from different combinations of these few ingredients.

Kofi blew out a long breath and watched it cloud in the cool air, and Zainab told him that the air around them is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen. Each breath contains more atoms than he could ever count, and since atoms are never used up, many of them have been recycled through plants, animals, oceans and storms for billions of years. He was, in all likelihood, breathing atoms that had once passed through the lungs of dinosaurs and the leaves of ancient trees.

The outermost electrons of an atom decide how it behaves toward its neighbours, and atoms often join together by sharing these electrons to form molecules. A molecule of water consists of one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, and the shared electrons act as a kind of glue, so that the properties of water are quite different from those of either gas. Chemistry, in the end, is little more than the physics of electrons as they are shared and swapped between atoms.

In a metal such as copper, each atom lets go of one or two of its outer electrons, which then wander freely among the atoms like a crowd in a market square. A battery can push this crowd along a wire to make a current, whereas in rubber and plastic the electrons are held fast, which explains why those materials are insulators. Zainab was pleased to see that she had linked her fifth idea so neatly to her sixth one.

Atoms are too small to be seen with light, but since the 1980s the scanning tunnelling microscope has felt the surface of a material with a needle so fine that it can picture individual atoms. In 1989 researchers at IBM even moved thirty-five xenon atoms one by one to spell the three letters of their company's name. Kofi was glad to learn that the atoms could be looked at as well as imagined.

The nuclei of some kinds of atom are unstable, and over time they break apart and give off energy in the form of radiation, which we call radioactivity. Zainab said that it happens quite naturally, in rocks, in soil and even inside our own bodies, and that no heat, cold or chemical treatment can speed it up or slow it down. The unstable atom simply changes at a moment that nobody can predict, as if it had decided on its own.

At the end of the nineteenth century the Polish-born scientist Marie Curie, working in Paris with her husband Pierre, studied the strange rays given off by uranium and coined the word radioactivity. She discovered two new elements, polonium and radium, and became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, one in physics in 1903 and one in chemistry in 1911. Her notebooks are still so radioactive today that they have to be kept in special boxes lined with lead.

Scientists sorted the radiation from unstable nuclei into three kinds, which they named alpha, beta and gamma after the first letters of the Greek alphabet. Alpha particles can be stopped by a sheet of paper, beta particles by a thin plate of aluminium, and the penetrating gamma rays, a very short wave of light, need several centimetres of lead. Radiation is dangerous only when it is strong or when the dose is large.

Although nobody can predict when a single atom will decay, a large sample behaves predictably, and the time in which half of the atoms change is called the half-life. Radioactive carbon fourteen has a half-life of about five thousand seven hundred years, so archaeologists can measure how much is left in an old piece of wood or bone and work out its age. The method works for samples up to about fifty thousand years old, and it is a clock that nobody ever has to wind.

Radiation is not merely a feature of laboratories, for every one of us is exposed to a small background amount from the rocks and soil, from cosmic rays arriving from space, and even from the food we eat. A banana, for instance, contains a trace of radioactive potassium, but the dose is minuscule and entirely harmless, and Kofi relaxed visibly when he heard it. What matters, said Zainab, is the size of the dose and not the mere presence of radiation.

In the 1930s scientists discovered that a heavy nucleus such as uranium can be split in two when a neutron strikes it, in a process that was named fission after the way living cells divide. The split releases a great deal of energy and two or three more neutrons, which can strike other nuclei in turn and start a chain reaction, either controlled in a reactor or let loose in a weapon. The physicists Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch worked out the correct explanation of the discovery in early 1939.

In a nuclear power station the chain reaction is held steady by control rods that absorb extra neutrons, and the heat it produces turns water into steam that spins a turbine connected to a generator. Nuclear plants provide roughly a tenth of the world's electricity and release no carbon dioxide while they run, although they also produce radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for a very long time. People still disagree strongly about how large a part nuclear stations should play in the energy of the future.

In 1905 Albert Einstein discovered that mass and energy are two faces of one thing, and his famous equation states that the energy equals the mass multiplied by the speed of light squared. Because the speed of light is so enormous, even one gram of matter, completely converted, would release about ninety trillion joules, which is roughly as much as a large power station makes in a day. A nucleus that splits ends up slightly lighter than before, and the missing mass is the energy.

Fusion is the opposite of fission, for it joins two light nuclei into a single heavier one and releases a tremendous amount of energy in the process. Deep inside the Sun, where the temperature is about fifteen million degrees, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, and every second about four million tonnes of the Sun's mass are converted into the light and heat that reach us. This is why Zainab liked to call sunshine nuclear power delivered at a safe distance of a hundred and fifty million kilometres.

Physicists around the world are trying to build fusion reactors that would copy the Sun, using magnets to hold a gas hotter than one hundred million degrees in a doughnut-shaped chamber. Fusion would use plentiful fuel and leave far less long-lived waste than fission, but keeping the gas hot and steady is extremely difficult, and no reactor has yet delivered useful electricity. Kofi thought it was a wonderfully brave idea to try to bottle a star, and he hoped that someone would succeed.

Zainab began the last part of her sixth idea by saying that at the smallest scale the world behaves in a way that nobody would guess. Light arrives in tiny packets of energy called photons, and when a single photon strikes a piece of metal it can knock an electron loose, which was explained by Einstein in 1905 and won him his Nobel Prize in 1921. This branch of science, which deals with the very small, is called quantum physics, and it is full of surprises.

On a smooth ramp you can stand at any height you like, but on a staircase you can only stand on the steps, and Zainab said that energy in the world of atoms behaves like a staircase.
