The German physicist Max Planck first proposed in 1900 that energy is handed out in small separate amounts, which he called quanta, and the electrons in an atom may only have certain particular amounts of energy. The idea seemed absurd to many people at first, and it was accepted only when the evidence became overwhelming.

When an electron in an atom drops from a higher energy step to a lower one, the atom gives off a single photon whose colour depends exactly on the size of the drop. Every element therefore has its own pattern of colours, which explains the red of a neon sign, the green of a firework and the yellow of salt thrown into a flame. Astronomers use the same patterns to find out what the distant stars are made of.

One of the strangest discoveries of the twentieth century was that a tiny thing can behave like a wave in some experiments and like a particle in others. When electrons are fired one by one at a screen with two narrow slits, they build up a pattern of stripes, which is the signature of waves interfering, even though each electron arrives at a single point. Nobody has yet found a simple everyday picture that explains both of these behaviours at the same time.

The wave nature of the electron is not merely a curiosity, for it is the basis of a very practical machine, the electron microscope. Because the waves associated with fast electrons are far shorter than the waves of visible light, the microscope can reveal details thousands of times smaller than any ordinary one, including viruses and the structure of cells. A twelve-year-old with a good idea, Zainab remarked, might use the machine to see the invisible.

In 1927 the German physicist Werner Heisenberg showed that we can never know both the exact position and the exact velocity of a tiny particle at the same time. The more precisely you pin down one, the vaguer the other becomes, and this uncertainty is not caused by clumsy instruments but is built into the way nature works. A particle is therefore better pictured as a blur of possibilities than as a tiny ball that follows a single path.

Take two identical radioactive atoms, and one may decay within a second while the other lasts for thousands of years, with nothing at all to tell them apart beforehand. Quantum physics can predict the odds with astonishing accuracy, but not the outcome of a single event, which makes the tiny world a place of chance rather than of certainty. Even Einstein disliked the idea, and he said that he did not believe that God plays dice.

A particle that is blurred into a cloud of possibilities has a small chance of turning up on the other side of a barrier that it seems to lack the energy to cross, a phenomenon called quantum tunnelling. It sounds like a fairy tale, but the Sun depends on it, for the hydrogen nuclei in its core are not quite energetic enough to meet and fuse without this strange shortcut. Without these odd rules of the very tiny, there would be no sunlight to warm the Earth at all.

Strange as the quantum world is, its rules are among the most thoroughly tested in all of science, and they make possible a long list of everyday machines. The transistors in a computer chip, the lasers that read barcodes and carry internet signals, the LEDs in a bulb, the cells of a solar panel and the scanners in a hospital all work only because electrons obey quantum laws. Kofi's own phone, Zainab told him, was really a pocket full of quantum physics, working quietly all day.

Inside a modern smartphone there are billions of transistors, each a tiny switch made from silicon, and they are so small that many fit across the width of a virus. The map that Kofi opened to find the way home relies on satellites carrying atomic clocks, whose ticking is governed by the exact energy steps of an atom. Physicists agree on the mathematics of the quantum world, Zainab added, but still argue about what it means.

The rain had stopped and the air smelled fresh, so Kofi and Zainab carried a blanket up the hill behind the house, with Ama and Biscuit following close behind. Far from the street lights the darkness was deep, and as their eyes adjusted the stars came out in their thousands, more than Kofi had ever noticed from the town. Zainab said that the sky was the best place to check the day's lessons.

Light is fast, but the stars are so far away that astronomers measure distances in light-years, the distance that light covers in a year, which is about nine and a half million million kilometres. The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about four light-years away, so the light now reaching Kofi's eyes left it more than four years ago. To look at the stars, therefore, is to look back in time, and each point of light shows a different past.

Each star is a gigantic ball of gas that is held together by its own gravity, which is the first idea in action on the largest scale. At the centre the fusion of nuclei, which is the last idea, releases heat that pushes outward and balances the inward pull, so that the star can shine steadily for millions or billions of years. When the fuel runs low, the balance is lost, and the star changes dramatically.

If you look carefully, said Zainab, you will see that stars are not all the same colour, and that the colour tells us the temperature of the surface. A very hot star glows blue-white, a cooler one such as our own Sun looks yellow, and the coolest look red, in the same way that an iron poker glows red when warm and whiter as it gets hotter. Heat and light, her third idea and her fourth, were working together overhead in every colour of the night sky.

Zainab pointed to a bright light low in the sky that shone steadily instead of twinkling, and told Kofi that it was a planet. Planets make no light of their own but reflect the sunshine that falls on them, and they stay in orbit around the Sun for the same reason that the Moon stays around the Earth. The first idea, motion and forces, was still quietly guiding everything that moved across the sky.

Kofi learned that the first atoms to appear after the beginning of the universe were nearly all hydrogen and helium, and that the heavier ones were built later, inside stars, by fusion. When old stars ran out of fuel and exploded, they scattered those atoms across space, and in time some of them gathered into the Earth, the oceans, the plants and eventually into the cells of every living thing. In that sense, Zainab said, every one of us is made of stardust, and so is everything we have ever touched.

The Sun is only one of a few hundred billion stars that form our galaxy, which is called the Milky Way, and beyond it lie billions of other galaxies. The most distant thing that a person can see with the unaided eye is the Andromeda galaxy, a faint smudge about two and a half million light-years away, and Zainab helped Kofi to find it on a dark night. The light that he saw had begun its journey long before any human beings existed on the Earth.

Astronomers have measured that the universe began roughly thirteen billion eight hundred million years ago and that it is still expanding, so that the distant galaxies are moving away from one another. Physics is far from finished, for no one yet knows what most of the universe is made of, or how to join quantum physics with gravity in a single theory. Zainab said that every unsolved puzzle is an invitation, and Kofi noticed that she was smiling.

Kofi pulled the crumpled envelope from his pocket, held it close to the torch, and crossed off the last of the six lines. In a single day he had met motion and forces, energy, heat, waves, electricity and magnetism, and the atoms inside everything, and none of it had needed a laboratory or a white coat. All it had needed, he realised, was a bicycle, a few tools, a patient aunt, and a habit of asking why.

Kofi and Zainab lay side by side on the blanket with their hands behind their heads, and neither of them spoke for a long while as the stars wheeled slowly overhead. The same six ideas that explained a bicycle ride, a boiling kettle, a pond and a thunderstorm also explained the distant stars, and the thought made the whole universe seem friendlier and more familiar. “Aunt Zainab,” Kofi whispered at last, with his eyes still fixed on the stars above, “what shall we ask tomorrow?”
